board_events.text: Elasticity: the tendency to spring back
Remove the deforming force and the body regains its original shape and size.
The opposite extreme is plasticity: wet clay or chewing gum keeps whatever shape you force on it.

board_events.text: For the same pull, steel resists deformation far more and snaps back more faithfully than rubber.
Trap: 'stretches more' is NOT 'more elastic'.
Elasticity measures the STRENGTH of the restoring tendency, not the SIZE of the stretch.

segments.text: <curious>Pick up a steel ruler and a rubber band and pull on both. The property we are watching when they spring back is elasticity, and this whole chapter rests on getting it right.
Here is the clean definition: elasticity is the property by which a body regains its original shape and size the instant the deforming force is removed.
The opposite personality is plasticity. Wet clay, chewing gum, or a lump of dough simply holds whatever new shape you force on it, and most real solids live somewhere between these two extremes.
Now look at this picture, because it captures the single biggest misconception. Same load hangs from a rubber wire and a steel wire, but the rubber stretches enormously while the steel barely moves.

In everyday language we would call the rubber more elastic because it stretches more. Physics says the exact opposite: for the same pull, steel resists deformation far more and returns to its length more faithfully.
<whisper>So hold on to this: stretching more does not mean more elastic. It is the most common conceptual trap in the chapter.
Elasticity is about the strength of the restoring tendency, not the size of the stretch. By that measure steel beats rubber every time.
<curious>एक steel ruler और एक rubber band उठाइए और दोनों को खींचिए। जब वो वापस अपनी शेप में आते हैं, वो property है elasticity, और पूरा chapter इसी पर टिका है।
साफ definition यह है: elasticity वो property है जिससे body, deforming force हटते ही अपनी original shape और size वापस पा लेती है।
इसका opposite है plasticity। गीली clay, chewing gum, या आटे का लोंदा — जो शेप दे दो वही रख लेते हैं, और ज़्यादातर real solids इन दोनों के बीच कहीं होते हैं।
अब इस picture को देखिए, क्योंकि यह सबसे बड़ी गलतफहमी पकड़ती है। same load rubber wire और steel wire से लटका है, पर rubber बहुत ज़्यादा खिंचता है और steel मुश्किल से हिलता है।

रोज़मर्रा की भाषा में हम rubber को more elastic कहेंगे क्योंकि वो ज़्यादा खिंचता है। physics बिलकुल उल्टा कहती है: same pull पर steel deformation को कहीं ज़्यादा resist करता है और ज़्यादा faithfully वापस आता है।
<whisper>तो यह याद रखिए: ज़्यादा खिंचना more elastic होना नहीं है। यह chapter का सबसे common trap है।
elasticity का मतलब है restoring tendency की strength, न कि stretch का size। इस पैमाने पर steel हर बार rubber को हराता है।

board_events.text: Picture the atoms of a solid connected by countless inter-atomic bonds, each a tiny spring.
At rest, every spring sits at its natural length and pushes with zero net force.
Apply a force and you stretch or squeeze these springs; like any spring, they push back.
This collective push-back IS the internal restoring force.
Pull harder and the springs stretch more and push back harder, up to the elastic limit.

segments.text: So what is actually happening inside the material when it springs back? Let us zoom all the way in to the atoms.
This picture is the mental model to carry through the whole chapter: the atoms sit at fixed positions, joined by inter-atomic bonds, and each bond behaves like a tiny spring.
Imagine countless of these molecular springs threading through the solid in every direction. That mesh of springs is what gives a solid its stiffness.
At rest, every spring sits at its natural length, so the net force is zero and nothing wants to move.
The moment you apply a force, you stretch or squeeze these springs, and exactly like any spring, they immediately push back against you.
That collective push-back from all the bonds is the body's internal restoring force. It is not magic; it is simply a great many little springs resisting at once.
Pull harder and the springs stretch further and push back harder, and this tidy proportional behaviour holds right up until the elastic limit, where the picture starts to break.
तो जब material वापस आता है तो अंदर हो क्या रहा है? चलिए पूरी तरह atoms तक zoom करते हैं।
यह picture पूरे chapter का mental model है: atoms fixed positions पर बैठे होते हैं, inter-atomic bonds से जुड़े, और हर bond एक tiny spring की तरह behave करता है।
कल्पना कीजिए ऐसे अनगिनत molecular springs solid में हर दिशा में फैले हुए हैं। यही springs का जाल solid को उसकी stiffness देता है।
आराम की हालत में हर spring अपनी natural length पर होती है, इसलिए net force zero है और कुछ हिलना नहीं चाहता।
जैसे ही आप force लगाते हैं, ये springs खिंचती या दबती हैं, और बिलकुल किसी spring की तरह वो तुरंत आप पर वापस push करती हैं।
सभी bonds का यह मिलाजुला push-back ही body का internal restoring force है। यह कोई जादू नहीं — बस बहुत सारी छोटी springs एक साथ resist कर रही हैं।
ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खींचिए तो springs और खिंचती हैं और और ज़ोर से push करती हैं, और यह साफ़ proportional behaviour elastic limit तक चलता है, जहाँ यह तस्वीर टूटने लगती है।

sections.title: Stress: restoring force per unit area

board_events.text: Stress: the cause, spread over area
A thick cable and a thin wire of the same steel bear different forces, so raw force is a bad measure.
Stress = restoring force per unit area of cross-section, equal in magnitude to the applied force at equilibrium.

Market analogy: stress is price per kilogram, not the total bill.

segments.text: Now we need a fair way to compare materials, and that starts with the idea of stress.
Here is the problem. A thick steel cable obviously withstands more force than a thin steel wire, yet they are the same material, so raw force alone tells us nothing about the material itself.
The fix is to divide by area. Stress is the restoring force per unit area of cross-section, and at equilibrium its magnitude equals the applied force divided by that area.
In symbols, stress sigma equals force F over area A. This single ratio is what lets us talk about the material, independent of how thick our sample happens to be.
Stress comes in three flavours, shown here. Study the picture, because each type reappears with its own modulus later.

Longitudinal stress acts along the axis, either stretching or squeezing. Volumetric stress is an all-around pressure on every face. Shear stress is a force acting parallel to a face, sliding it sideways.
The S I unit of stress is the pascal, which is one newton per square metre, and its dimensional formula is M, L to the minus one, T to the minus two.
A market analogy fixes it in memory: stress is like the price per kilogram of vegetables, the force spread over area, not the total bill.
अब हमें materials को fairly compare करने का तरीका चाहिए, और यह शुरू होता है stress के idea से।
problem यह है। एक मोटी steel cable एक पतली steel wire से ज़्यादा force झेलती है, फिर भी दोनों same material हैं, तो अकेला raw force material के बारे में कुछ नहीं बताता।
इसका हल है area से divide करना। stress है restoring force per unit area of cross-section, और equilibrium पर इसकी magnitude applied force को area से divide करने के बराबर होती है।
symbols में, stress sigma बराबर force F बटा area A. यही एक ratio हमें material की बात करने देता है, चाहे sample कितना भी मोटा हो।
stress तीन तरह का होता है, यहाँ दिखाया गया है। picture ध्यान से देखिए, क्योंकि हर type आगे अपने modulus के साथ लौटता है।
longitudinal stress axis के साथ लगता है, या तो खींचते या दबाते हुए। volumetric stress हर face पर all-around pressure है। shear stress किसी face के parallel लगता है, उसे sideways खिसकाते हुए।
stress की S I unit है pascal, यानी one newton per square metre, और इसका dimensional formula है M, L to the minus one, T to the minus two.
एक market analogy इसे याद रखा देती है: stress सब्ज़ी के price per kilogram जैसा है, force जो area पर फैला है, न कि पूरा bill।

A ten metre wire stretching one centimetre differs from a ten centimetre wire stretching one centimetre.
Strain = change in a dimension as a fraction of the original dimension.

board_events.text: Longitudinal strain is $\Delta L/L$; volume strain is $\Delta V/V$; shear strain is $\phi = x/h$ in radians.
Strain is a pure ratio: dimensionless, no unit, never in pascals.
Stress is the cause per unit area; strain is the effect per unit size. Both are ratios, so both compare fairly.

segments.text: Stress fixed the cause; now we normalise the effect, and that gives us strain.

Think about why raw elongation is misleading. A ten metre wire that stretches by one centimetre is barely disturbed, while a ten centimetre wire stretching the same one centimetre is stretched hugely.
So we measure the change as a fraction of the original size. Strain is the change in a dimension divided by the original dimension.
Written out, strain epsilon equals the change in a dimension over the original dimension. That fraction is what makes long and short samples comparable.
Like stress, strain comes in three matching types, shown here, one for each type of stress.
Longitudinal strain is delta L over L. Volume strain is delta V over V. Shear strain is phi, equal to the sideways slide x over the separation h, and it is measured in radians.
<excited>Here is a favourite exam point: strain is a pure ratio, so it is completely dimensionless. It carries no unit at all, no pascals, no metres.
Put it together: stress is the cause per unit area, strain is the effect per unit size. Because both are ratios, they let us compare the material itself rather than the lump we happen to hold.
stress ने cause को fix किया; अब हम effect को normalise करते हैं, और वो देता है strain.
सोचिए raw elongation क्यों गुमराह करता है। दस मीटर की wire जो एक centimetre खिंचे वो मुश्किल से disturb हुई, जबकि दस centimetre की wire वही एक centimetre खिंचे तो बहुत ज़्यादा खिंच गई।
इसलिए हम change को original size के fraction के रूप में नापते हैं। strain है किसी dimension का change बटा original dimension.
लिखें तो, strain epsilon बराबर change in a dimension बटा original dimension. यही fraction लंबे और छोटे samples को comparable बनाता है।
stress की तरह strain भी तीन matching types में आता है, यहाँ दिखाया गया, हर stress के लिए एक।
longitudinal strain है delta L बटा L. volume strain है delta V बटा V. shear strain है phi, यानी sideways slide x बटा separation h, और यह radians में नापा जाता है।
<excited>यहाँ एक favourite exam point है: strain एक pure ratio है, इसलिए पूरी तरह dimensionless है। इसकी कोई unit नहीं, न pascals, न metres.
जोड़िए: stress है cause per unit area, strain है effect per unit size. दोनों ratios हैं, इसलिए वो हमें उस लोंदे की जगह खुद material को compare करने देते हैं।

sections.title: Hooke's law and the modulus of elasticity

board_events.text: Hooke's law: stress proportional to strain
Within the elastic limit, stress and strain rise in strict proportion.
E is the modulus of elasticity, a property of the MATERIAL only, independent of shape or size.
Unit of E: pascal. Dimensions $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
The proportionality holds ONLY within the elastic limit.
Past that limit the line bends, the body keeps a permanent set, and eventually it fractures.

segments.text: With stress and strain defined, we can state the law that ties them together: Hooke's law.
The statement is simple. As long as we stay within the elastic limit, stress and strain rise in strict proportion to each other.
In symbols, sigma is proportional to epsilon, which we write as sigma equals E times epsilon. E is the constant that turns that proportionality into an equation.
This E is the modulus of elasticity, and the key fact is that it depends on the material alone. Change the shape or the size and E does not budge.
Because strain is dimensionless, E carries the same unit and dimensions as stress: the pascal, with dimensions M, L to the minus one, T to the minus two.
<whisper>But never forget the fine print on this law: it holds only within the elastic limit.
Push a material past that limit and three things break our tidy picture: the proportionality fails, the body no longer fully returns, keeping a permanent set, and eventually it fractures.
stress और strain define होने के बाद, हम वो law बता सकते हैं जो इन्हें जोड़ता है: Hooke's law.
statement सरल है। जब तक हम elastic limit के अंदर रहते हैं, stress और strain एक-दूसरे के strict proportion में बढ़ते हैं।
symbols में, sigma proportional है epsilon के, जिसे हम लिखते हैं sigma बराबर E times epsilon. E वो constant है जो इस proportionality को equation बना देता है।
यह E है modulus of elasticity, और सबसे ज़रूरी बात यह है कि यह सिर्फ़ material पर depend करता है। shape या size बदलिए, E टस से मस नहीं होता।
चूँकि strain dimensionless है, E की unit और dimensions stress जैसी ही हैं: pascal, dimensions M, L to the minus one, T to the minus two.
<whisper>पर इस law की fine print कभी मत भूलिए: यह सिर्फ़ elastic limit के अंदर चलता है।

board_events.text: In equilibrium the upward restoring force balances the weight, so the stretching force is $F = Mg$.
Divide stress by strain, by the definition of Young's modulus.
This is the working formula behind Searle's experiment.
Y contains only material and geometry inputs you can measure; it does not care how the wire is loaded.

segments.text: Let us derive Young's modulus from scratch for the simplest possible setup, a hanging wire.
Here is the arrangement: a wire of natural length L and radius r, clamped rigidly at the top, with a mass M hung from the lower end.
In equilibrium the wire is not accelerating, so the upward restoring force must balance the downward weight exactly. That means the stretching force F equals M g.
From there the stress is the force over the area, M g over pi r squared, and the longitudinal strain is the elongation delta L over the original length L.
Young's modulus is defined as stress over strain, so we simply divide the two expressions we just wrote.
Carrying out that division gives Y equals M g L over pi r squared delta L. That is the master result for a loaded wire.
<curious>Notice what this formula is: it is exactly the working equation behind Searle's experiment, the standard lab method for measuring Young's modulus.
And notice what it contains: only measurable material and geometry inputs. It does not depend on how the wire is loaded, only on the material, which is precisely why it is a property of the material.
चलिए सबसे सरल setup, एक hanging wire, के लिए Young's modulus को शुरू से derive करते हैं।
arrangement यह है: natural length L और radius r की wire, ऊपर से rigidly clamped, और नीचे के सिरे से mass M लटका हुआ।
equilibrium में wire accelerate नहीं कर रही, इसलिए upward restoring force को downward weight को बिलकुल balance करना है। मतलब stretching force F बराबर M g.
यहाँ से stress है force बटा area, M g बटा pi r squared, और longitudinal strain है elongation delta L बटा original length L.
Young's modulus की definition है stress बटा strain, तो हम बस अभी लिखे दोनों expressions को divide कर देते हैं।
यह division देता है Y बराबर M g L बटा pi r squared delta L. यही loaded wire का master result है।
<curious>ध्यान दीजिए यह formula क्या है: यह ठीक Searle's experiment के पीछे की working equation है, Young's modulus नापने का standard lab तरीका।
और ध्यान दीजिए इसमें क्या है: सिर्फ़ measurable material और geometry inputs. यह इस बात पर depend नहीं करता कि wire कैसे load हुई, सिर्फ़ material पर — इसीलिए यह material की property है।

board_events.text: The 1/2 means the whole weight effectively acts at the centre of mass.
That 'average tension' shortcut, effective length $L/2$, saves real time in exams.

segments.text: Now a subtler cousin of the same problem: what if the rod stretches under nothing but its own weight?
The picture makes the key idea visible. The top of the rod carries everything hanging below it, while the very bottom carries almost nothing, so the tension varies with height.
So remove the external mass entirely. Each part of the rod is now loaded by the material beneath it, and that is why the tension is not uniform along its length.
Take a thin element of thickness d x at a height x measured from the bottom. The force it must support is the weight of all the rod below it.
That weight is rho A x g, so the little element feels a stress rho x g, a strain rho x g over Y, and stretches by rho x g over Y times d x.
Now add up every element by integrating from zero to L. The result is delta L equals rho g L squared over two Y, which is also M g L over two A Y.
<curious>Look closely at that factor of one half. It says the rod stretches exactly as if its entire weight acted at its centre of mass, halfway down.
That is the average-tension shortcut: treat the self-weight as a point load at an effective length of L over two. Recognising it turns an integral into a one-line answer under exam pressure.
अब उसी problem का एक बारीक cousin: अगर rod सिर्फ़ अपने खुद के weight से खिंचे तो?
picture मुख्य idea दिखा देती है। rod का ऊपरी हिस्सा नीचे लटकते सब कुछ को झेलता है, जबकि सबसे नीचे लगभग कुछ नहीं, इसलिए tension height के साथ बदलता है।
तो external mass पूरी तरह हटा दीजिए। rod का हर हिस्सा अब अपने नीचे के material से load होता है, इसीलिए tension पूरी length में uniform नहीं है।
नीचे से नापी गई height x पर thickness d x का एक पतला element लीजिए। जो force इसे झेलना है वो है इसके नीचे के पूरे rod का weight.
वो weight है rho A x g, तो छोटा element महसूस करता है stress rho x g, strain rho x g बटा Y, और खिंचता है rho x g बटा Y times d x.
अब हर element को zero से L तक integrate करके जोड़िए। नतीजा है delta L बराबर rho g L squared बटा two Y, जो M g L बटा two A Y भी है।
<curious>उस one-half factor को ध्यान से देखिए। यह कहता है rod ठीक वैसे खिंचता है जैसे उसका पूरा weight उसके centre of mass पर, आधी ऊँचाई पर, लगा हो।
यही average-tension shortcut है: self-weight को L बटा two की effective length पर एक point load मानिए। इसे पहचानना exam में एक integral को one-line answer बना देता है।

segments.text: This single graph is the map of the whole chapter, so let us trace it carefully from left to right.
Study the picture: the green band on the left is elastic behaviour, the orange band on the right is plastic, and five landmarks are labelled along the way.
The first stretch, O to P, is a straight line. Here Hooke's law holds perfectly, and the slope of that line is the Young's modulus of the material.
Just beyond P is E, the elastic limit. Up to here the material still returns to its original shape, but the line is no longer perfectly straight.
Then comes the yield point, and this is the turning of the story. Strain suddenly shoots up for very little extra stress, and permanent deformation, the plastic region, begins.
The curve rises gently to a peak, the ultimate tensile strength, the greatest stress the material can bear. Past the peak it sags and finally reaches the fracture point, where it snaps.

<whisper>Here is how the graph sorts materials: a ductile metal like copper or steel has a long plastic region between yield and fracture, while a brittle solid like glass fractures almost immediately after the elastic limit.
One more reading: the area under the curve up to any point equals the energy absorbed per unit volume, a fact we will lean on heavily when we reach elastic energy.

sections.title: Young's, bulk, rigidity and Poisson's ratio

board_events.text: The four elastic constants
Young's modulus Y: longitudinal stress over longitudinal strain.
Bulk modulus B: volume stress over volume strain; the minus sign shows volume falls as pressure rises. For a gas, isothermal $B=P$, adiabatic $B=\gamma P$.
Rigidity $\eta$: shear stress over shear strain. Poisson's ratio $\nu$: lateral over longitudinal strain, dimensionless, typically between 0.2 and 0.4 for metals.
Solids have all three moduli; liquids and gases have only bulk modulus.

segments.text: Now the toolkit. Each type of deformation gets its own stiffness number, and here are all four constants on one board.
First, Young's modulus. It is longitudinal stress over longitudinal strain, and for a loaded wire it works out to F L over A delta L, or M g L over pi r squared delta L.
So Young's modulus Y answers the stretching question: how hard does this material resist being lengthened.
Second, the bulk modulus. It is minus pressure over fractional volume change, or minus V times d P by d V, and its reciprocal is the compressibility k.

Bulk modulus B answers the squeezing question. The minus sign simply records that volume decreases as pressure increases. For a gas B is not fixed: it equals P when the change is slow and isothermal, and gamma P when it is sudden and adiabatic.
Third and fourth: the modulus of rigidity eta, which is shear stress over shear strain, and Poisson's ratio nu, minus the lateral strain over the longitudinal strain.
Rigidity eta answers the shape-change question. Poisson's ratio nu is dimensionless and for most metals sits between roughly zero point two and zero point four.
<excited>One structural fact ties it together: solids possess all three moduli, but liquids and gases possess only the bulk modulus, because they cannot sustain a shear.
अब toolkit. हर तरह के deformation को अपना stiffness number मिलता है, और यहाँ चारों constants एक ही board पर हैं।
पहला, Young's modulus. यह है longitudinal stress बटा longitudinal strain, और loaded wire के लिए यह बनता है F L बटा A delta L, या M g L बटा pi r squared delta L.
तो Young's modulus Y stretching का सवाल answer करता है: यह material लंबा होने को कितनी मेहनत से resist करता है।
दूसरा, bulk modulus. यह है minus pressure बटा fractional volume change, या minus V times d P by d V, और इसका reciprocal है compressibility k.

bulk modulus B squeezing का सवाल answer करता है। minus sign बस यह दर्ज करता है कि pressure बढ़ने पर volume घटता है। gas के लिए B fixed नहीं: slow isothermal change पर यह P के बराबर, और sudden adiabatic पर gamma P.
तीसरा और चौथा: modulus of rigidity eta, जो है shear stress बटा shear strain, और Poisson's ratio nu, minus lateral strain बटा longitudinal strain.
rigidity eta shape-change का सवाल answer करता है। Poisson's ratio nu dimensionless है और ज़्यादातर metals के लिए लगभग zero point two से zero point four के बीच रहता है।
<excited>एक structural fact सब जोड़ देता है: solids के पास तीनों moduli होते हैं, पर liquids और gases के पास सिर्फ़ bulk modulus, क्योंकि वो shear नहीं झेल सकते।

sections.title: CBSE: Young's modulus of a steel wire

board_events.text: CBSE example: Young's modulus of a steel wire
Given: L = 3.0 m, A = 2.0 mm-squared, elongation = 0.60 mm, load = 8.0 kg, g = 10 m/s-squared.
First find the stretching force from the load.
Convert to S I units: A = 2.0e-6 m-squared and elongation = 6.0e-4 m, then apply the formula.
Matches the textbook value for steel. Always carry the unit into the final line.

segments.text: Let us put the formula to work on a clean board-level numerical.

The data: a steel wire three point zero metres long, cross-section two point zero square millimetres, stretching by zero point six zero millimetres under an eight point zero kilogram load, with g taken as ten metres per second squared.
The first move is always the same: find the actual stretching force, which is just the weight of the load.
Force equals M g, that is eight point zero times ten, which gives eighty newtons.

Before substituting, convert everything to S I units. The area becomes two point zero times ten to the minus six square metres, and the elongation becomes six point zero times ten to the minus four metres.
Now plug into Young's modulus equals F L over A delta L: that is eighty times three point zero, divided by the product of the area and the elongation.
The arithmetic gives two hundred forty over one point two times ten to the minus nine, which comes out to two point zero times ten to the power eleven pascals.
<excited>That is exactly the accepted textbook value for steel, a lovely sanity check. And notice the discipline: carry the unit, pascals, right into the final line, every time.
चलिए formula को एक साफ़ board-level numerical पर लगाते हैं।

data: steel wire three point zero metres लंबी, cross-section two point zero square millimetres, eight point zero kilogram load पर zero point six zero millimetres खिंचती है, g को ten metres per second squared लेते हुए।
पहला कदम हमेशा एक ही: असली stretching force निकालिए, जो बस load का weight है।
force बराबर M g, यानी eight point zero times ten, जो देता है eighty newtons.
substitute करने से पहले सब कुछ S I units में बदलिए। area बनता है two point zero times ten to the minus six square metres, और elongation बनता है six point zero times ten to the minus four metres.
अब Young's modulus बराबर F L बटा A delta L में रखिए: यानी eighty times three point zero, area और elongation के product से divide।
arithmetic देता है two hundred forty बटा one point two times ten to the minus nine, जो निकलता है two point zero times ten to the power eleven pascals.
<excited>यह ठीक steel का accepted textbook value है, एक बढ़िया sanity check. और यह discipline देखिए: unit, pascals, हर बार final line तक साथ ले जाइए।

board_events.text: Same material means Y is identical for both, so never compute it: cancel it right away.
A stretches twice as much: B is longer by two, but fatter by four in area, so the net effect is divide by two.
Both are the same material, so they are EQUALLY elastic. Geometry changes stretch, never elasticity.

segments.text: This is a classic N E E T trap, and the picture is where you win it before touching a calculator.

Two wires, A and B, same material, same load. Wire B is twice as long as A and has twice the radius. The question hides two traps: rushing to plug numbers, and confusing stretching more with being more elastic.
First insight: since the material is the same, Young's modulus is identical for both wires. So do not compute it; cancel it immediately and work with a proportionality.
From delta L equals F L over pi r squared Y, with force, Young's modulus and pi all common, elongation is proportional to length over radius squared.

Take the ratio for A over B. It is L over r squared, divided by two L over the square of two r. The four in the denominator turns two L over four r squared into L over two r squared, and the whole ratio collapses to two.

So A stretches twice as much as B. Feel it physically: B is longer, which alone would stretch it more, but B is also fatter, and area scales as radius squared, so four times the area wins, and the net effect is a factor of one half.

<whisper>Now the sting in the tail. A stretches more, but both are the same material with the same Young's modulus, so they are equally elastic. Geometry changes the stretch, never the elasticity, so eliminate any option that calls one more elastic.
यह एक classic N E E T trap है, और picture ही वो जगह है जहाँ आप calculator छूने से पहले जीत जाते हैं।
दो wires, A और B, same material, same load. wire B, A से दुगनी लंबी है और radius दुगना। सवाल में दो traps छिपे हैं: numbers plug करने की जल्दी, और ज़्यादा खिंचने को more elastic समझ लेना।
पहली insight: material same है, इसलिए Young's modulus दोनों wires के लिए identical है। तो इसे compute मत कीजिए; तुरंत cancel करके एक proportionality पर काम कीजिए।
delta L बराबर F L बटा pi r squared Y से, जहाँ force, Young's modulus और pi common हैं, elongation proportional है length बटा radius squared के।
A बटा B का ratio लीजिए। यह है L बटा r squared, बटा two L बटा square of two r. denominator का four, two L बटा four r squared को L बटा two r squared बना देता है, और पूरा ratio सिमटकर two रह जाता है।

तो A, B से दुगना खिंचता है। इसे physically महसूस कीजिए: B लंबा है, जो अकेले उसे ज़्यादा खींचता, पर B मोटा भी है, और area radius squared के हिसाब से बढ़ता है, तो चार गुना area जीतता है, net effect one half.

<whisper>अब पूँछ में डंक। A ज़्यादा खिंचता है, पर दोनों same material, same Young's modulus — इसलिए equally elastic. geometry stretch बदलती है, elasticity कभी नहीं, तो जो option किसी एक को more elastic कहे उसे हटा दीजिए।

board_events.text: Two ideas: wires in series carry the SAME tension, and the total elongation is the SUM.
They stretch equally here only by coincidence, not by any rule.

segments.text: Now a step up in level, a J E E Main composite. A steel wire is joined end-to-end to a copper wire, and a ten kilogram mass hangs from the bottom.
The figure shows the arrangement: steel on top with area A and modulus Y-steel, copper below with twice the area and half the modulus, and the load at the very bottom.
Two concepts unlock it. Because the wires are in series, both carry the same tension, and the total elongation is simply the sum of the two individual stretches.
The tension throughout equals M g, that is ten kilograms times ten, giving one hundred newtons in both wires.

For the steel piece, delta L is F L over A Y. That is one hundred times one point zero, over the product of one times ten to the minus six and two times ten to the power eleven, which is five point zero times ten to the minus four metres.

For the copper piece, the same formula with its own area and modulus, one hundred times one point zero over two times ten to the minus six times one times ten to the power eleven, also gives five point zero times ten to the minus four metres.
Adding the two stretches, the total elongation is one point zero times ten to the minus three metres, that is one point zero millimetres.
<curious>Do not over-read the fact that both pieces happened to stretch equally. Their length, modulus and area balances simply coincided here; it is a nice coincidence, not a rule to memorise.
अब level में एक कदम ऊपर, एक J E E Main composite. एक steel wire copper wire से end-to-end जुड़ी है, और नीचे से ten kilogram mass लटका है।
figure arrangement दिखाता है: ऊपर steel area A और modulus Y-steel के साथ, नीचे copper दुगने area और आधे modulus के साथ, और load बिलकुल नीचे।
दो concepts इसे खोलते हैं। wires series में हैं, इसलिए दोनों same tension झेलती हैं, और total elongation बस दोनों individual stretches का sum है।
पूरे में tension बराबर M g, यानी ten kilograms times ten, जो दोनों wires में one hundred newtons देता है।

steel piece के लिए delta L है F L बटा A Y. यानी one hundred times one point zero, बटा one times ten to the minus six और two times ten to the power eleven का product, जो है five point zero times ten to the minus four metres.

copper piece के लिए वही formula अपने area और modulus के साथ, one hundred times one point zero बटा two times ten to the minus six times one times ten to the power eleven, भी देता है five point zero times ten to the minus four metres.
दोनों stretches जोड़िए, total elongation है one point zero times ten to the minus three metres, यानी one point zero millimetres.
<curious>इस बात को ज़्यादा मत पढ़िए कि दोनों pieces बराबर खिंचे। उनके length, modulus और area के balances यहाँ बस मिल गए; यह एक अच्छा coincidence है, याद रखने वाला rule नहीं।

board_events.text: The tension is non-uniform: at distance x, it must supply the centripetal force for all mass beyond x.
The 1/3 (versus 1/2 for self-weight) comes from tension varying as x-squared, not x.

segments.text: Finally, the discriminator problem, a J E E Advanced rod spinning on a frictionless table about a vertical axis through one end.
The top view is the whole trick. At any distance x from the axis, the tension there has to supply the centripetal force for every bit of mass lying beyond x, out to the free end.
So the tension is non-uniform, largest at the axis and zero at the tip, exactly the opposite feel from a load hanging at the bottom.

Integrate the centripetal demand from x out to L, using linear mass density lambda equals M over L. The tension at x works out to M omega squared over two L, times the quantity L squared minus x squared.
Each element stretches by its stress over Y times d x. Integrating that tension across the whole rod gives delta L equals M omega squared L squared over three A Y.

Now the numbers: two point zero kilograms, omega ten radians per second, length one metre, area one times ten to the minus six, Young's modulus two times ten to the power eleven. That is two hundred over six times ten to the power five, about three point three times ten to the minus four metres, roughly zero point three three millimetres.

<whisper>Here is the discriminator. This answer carries a one third, where the self-weight problem carried a one half. The difference is that here the tension varies as x squared, quadratically, not linearly, and that is what separates students who memorise from students who derive.
आख़िर में, discriminator problem, एक J E E Advanced rod जो frictionless table पर एक सिरे से गुज़रती vertical axis के गिर्द घूम रही है।
top view ही पूरा trick है। axis से किसी भी distance x पर, वहाँ की tension को x के आगे पड़े हर mass के लिए centripetal force देना है, free end तक।
तो tension non-uniform है, axis पर सबसे ज़्यादा और tip पर zero, बिलकुल उल्टा feel जो नीचे लटके load से होता।
centripetal demand को x से L तक integrate कीजिए, linear mass density lambda बराबर M बटा L लेते हुए। x पर tension बनती है M omega squared बटा two L, times quantity L squared minus x squared.
हर element अपने stress बटा Y times d x जितना खिंचता है। उस tension को पूरे rod पर integrate करने से मिलता है delta L बराबर M omega squared L squared बटा three A Y.

अब numbers: two point zero kilograms, omega ten radians per second, length one metre, area one times ten to the minus six, Young's modulus two times ten to the power eleven. यानी two hundred बटा six times ten to the power five, लगभग three point three times ten to the minus four metres, करीब zero point three three millimetres.

<whisper>यहाँ discriminator है। इस answer में one third है, जहाँ self-weight problem में one half था। फ़र्क़ यह है कि यहाँ tension x squared की तरह, quadratically, बदलती है, linearly नहीं, और यही derive करने वालों को रटने वालों से अलग करता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and the same-material pro-tip

board_events.text: Common pitfalls and one pro-tip
Radius vs diameter: examiners quote the diameter. Halve it before squaring, or area is off by 4.
'More stretch equals more elastic' is wrong. Higher Young's modulus means more elastic.
Strain is a pure ratio: never write pascals or metres on it. Only stress and the moduli carry pascals.
Elastic energy uses the average force, one-half F, and self-weight elongation uses effective length L over 2.
Pro-tip: for same-material comparisons, never compute Y. Reduce to a proportionality.
A thirty-second ratio replaces a messy calculation, and you cannot slip on a number you never wrote.

segments.text: Let us close the subtopic by pinning down the traps that cost the most marks.

First and biggest: radius versus diameter. Examiners love quoting the diameter. Forget to halve it before squaring and your area is wrong by a factor of four, and your Young's modulus is wrong with it. Underline the word the moment you read it.
Second, the headline misconception again: more stretch does not mean more elastic. It is the higher Young's modulus that means more elastic, which is why steel beats rubber.
Third, never put units on strain. It is a pure ratio, dimensionless, with no pascals and no metres. Only stress and the three moduli carry the pascal.

Fourth, do not drop the one half. Elastic energy uses the average force, one half F times the stretch, and self-weight elongation uses an effective length of L over two. That one half is physics, not decoration.
<excited>And now the pro-tip that saves the most time: whenever a question says same material, never compute Young's modulus at all. Cancel it and reduce everything to a proportionality.
In practice that means writing delta L is proportional to L over r squared, or to F L over r squared, and then just taking the ratio the question asks for.
A thirty-second ratio replaces a messy two-line calculation, and the quiet bonus is that you cannot make an arithmetic slip on a number you never wrote down.
चलिए subtopic को उन traps पर उँगली रखते हुए बंद करते हैं जो सबसे ज़्यादा marks ले जाते हैं।

पहला और सबसे बड़ा: radius versus diameter. examiners diameter quote करना पसंद करते हैं। square करने से पहले उसे आधा करना भूले तो आपका area चार गुने factor से गलत, और साथ में Young's modulus भी। पढ़ते ही उस शब्द को underline कीजिए।
दूसरा, वही headline गलतफहमी दोबारा: ज़्यादा खिंचना more elastic नहीं है। more elastic का मतलब higher Young's modulus है, इसीलिए steel rubber को हराता है।
तीसरा, strain पर कभी unit मत लगाइए। यह एक pure ratio है, dimensionless, न pascals न metres. सिर्फ़ stress और तीनों moduli pascal रखते हैं।
चौथा, one half मत गिराइए। elastic energy average force लेती है, one half F times stretch, और self-weight elongation L बटा two की effective length लेती है। वो one half physics है, सजावट नहीं।
<excited>और अब वो pro-tip जो सबसे ज़्यादा समय बचाता है: जब भी सवाल कहे same material, Young's modulus कभी compute मत कीजिए। उसे cancel करके सब कुछ एक proportionality बना दीजिए।
practice में इसका मतलब है delta L proportional to L बटा r squared, या F L बटा r squared लिखना, और फिर बस वो ratio लेना जो सवाल माँगता है।
एक thirty-second ratio एक messy two-line calculation की जगह ले लेता है, और चुपचाप bonus यह कि जिस number को आपने लिखा ही नहीं उस पर arithmetic slip हो ही नहीं सकती।

board_events.text: The quantity in the bracket is exactly the spring constant, so every rod is a spring.
Short and fat is stiff: k grows as the wire gets shorter and thicker.
Now every spring rule from Class 11 mechanics transfers to wires.

segments.text: Subtopic one gave us the four elastic constants. Now we put them to work, and the first big idea unlocks half the chapter: a loaded wire is just a spring.
Start from something you already own. Young's modulus is F L over A delta L, a relation for a stretched wire.
Rearrange it to make the force the subject, and you get F equals the quantity Y A over L, times the elongation delta L.
Look at the picture. On the left is the wire with a load; on the right is an ordinary coil spring with the same load. They are mechanically the same object.
Because the force is that bracket times the stretch, the bracket is playing precisely the role of a spring constant. So every rod, every wire, is secretly a spring.
We give the bracket a name: the force constant k equals Y A over L. Read off its behaviour: k is proportional to area A, and inversely proportional to length L.
In words, short and fat is stiff. A thick, short wire has a large k; a long, thin one has a small k, which is why a crane cable is stiff and a guitar string is soft.
<excited>And here is the payoff: the entire toolkit of spring combinations you learned in Class eleven mechanics now transfers, unchanged, to any tangle of wires.
subtopic one ने हमें चार elastic constants दिए। अब हम इन्हें काम पर लगाते हैं, और पहला बड़ा idea आधा chapter खोल देता है: एक loaded wire बस एक spring है।
जो आपके पास पहले से है वहीं से शुरू कीजिए। Young's modulus है F L बटा A delta L, एक stretched wire का relation.
इसे rearrange करके force को subject बनाइए, और मिलता है F बराबर quantity Y A बटा L, times elongation delta L.
picture देखिए। बाईं ओर load के साथ wire है; दाईं ओर उसी load के साथ एक आम coil spring है। दोनों mechanically एक ही object हैं।
चूँकि force उस bracket times stretch है, वो bracket ठीक spring constant का role निभा रहा है। तो हर rod, हर wire, दरअसल एक spring है।
उस bracket को नाम देते हैं: force constant k बराबर Y A बटा L. इसका behaviour पढ़िए: k, area A के proportional है, और length L के inversely proportional.
शब्दों में, short and fat is stiff. एक मोटी, छोटी wire का k बड़ा; लंबी, पतली का छोटा, इसीलिए crane cable stiff है और guitar string soft.
<excited>और यहाँ payoff है: Class eleven mechanics में सीखा spring combinations का पूरा toolkit अब बिना बदले किसी भी wires के जाल पर transfer हो जाता है।

board_events.text: Wires joined end-to-end behave like springs in series: soft, they share the same force and add their stretches.
Wires placed side-by-side behave like springs in parallel: stiff, they share the same stretch and add their stiffnesses.
Bullock-cart ropes: tied one-after-another they sag, tied side-by-side they share the load.

segments.text: With the spring reinterpretation in hand, combining wires becomes effortless. There are exactly two ways to connect them.
The picture shows both. On the left, series; on the right, parallel. Keep this contrast in view for the whole subtopic.
First, wires joined end-to-end. They behave like springs in series: the lower one passes the full load up to the upper one, so both carry the same force, and their individual stretches simply add.
For series, the reciprocals of the stiffnesses add: one over k equivalent equals one over k one plus one over k two. Adding reciprocals always gives a softer, smaller equivalent stiffness.
Second, wires placed side-by-side sharing a load. They behave like springs in parallel: now both stretch by the same amount, and it is their stiffnesses that add directly.
For parallel, k equivalent equals k one plus k two. A bundle of parallel wires is stiffer than any single strand.

<curious>A bullock-cart picture nails it: two ropes tied one after another let the load sag and the weaker rope dominates, but the same ropes side-by-side share the strain and the pair is stronger than either alone.
spring reinterpretation हाथ में आते ही wires को combine करना आसान हो जाता है। इन्हें जोड़ने के ठीक दो तरीके हैं।
picture दोनों दिखाती है। बाईं ओर series; दाईं ओर parallel. इस contrast को पूरे subtopic के लिए नज़र में रखिए।
पहला, end-to-end जुड़ी wires। ये series springs की तरह behave करती हैं: नीचे वाली पूरा load ऊपर वाली तक पहुँचाती है, इसलिए दोनों same force झेलती हैं, और उनके individual stretches बस जुड़ जाते हैं।
series के लिए stiffnesses के reciprocals जुड़ते हैं: one over k equivalent बराबर one over k one plus one over k two. reciprocals जोड़ना हमेशा softer, छोटी equivalent stiffness देता है।
दूसरा, side-by-side रखी wires जो load बाँटती हैं। ये parallel springs की तरह behave करती हैं: अब दोनों same amount खिंचती हैं, और उनकी stiffnesses सीधे जुड़ती हैं।
parallel के लिए k equivalent बराबर k one plus k two. parallel wires का गुच्छा किसी एक strand से ज़्यादा stiff होता है।

<curious>एक बैलगाड़ी की तस्वीर इसे पक्का करती है: एक के बाद एक बँधी दो रस्सियाँ load को सैग करने देती हैं और कमज़ोर रस्सी हावी रहती है, पर वही रस्सियाँ side-by-side strain बाँट लेती हैं और जोड़ी किसी एक से मज़बूत होती है।

board_events.text: Both rods carry the same tension F, and the total stretch is the sum of the two.
The combined rod has length $2L$, area $A$, and some effective modulus $Y_{eq}$, so $k_{eq} = Y_{eq}A/2L$.
This is NOT the arithmetic mean of Y1 and Y2, a favourite exam trap.

segments.text: Let us derive a result that examiners love to test: the equivalent Young's modulus of two rods joined end-to-end.
The setup, shown here: two rods of equal length L and equal area A, but different moduli Y one and Y two, welded into a single rod of length two L.
Because this is a series arrangement, both rods carry the same tension F, and the total stretch is the sum of the two individual stretches.
So the reciprocal stiffnesses add, and each rod has k equal to its own Y times A over L. Write that down as the starting equation.
Now treat the combined rod as one object: it has length two L, the same area A, and some effective modulus Y equivalent, so its stiffness is Y equivalent times A over two L.

Substitute and the areas and lengths cancel neatly, giving two over Y equivalent equals one over Y one plus one over Y two, which rearranges to Y equivalent equals two Y one Y two over the sum Y one plus Y two.
<whisper>Burn this in: the answer is the harmonic-type combination, not the simple average of Y one and Y two. Writing the arithmetic mean is one of the most common mistakes in the whole chapter.
चलिए वो result derive करते हैं जिसे examiners test करना पसंद करते हैं: end-to-end जुड़े दो rods का equivalent Young's modulus.
setup, यहाँ दिखाया: equal length L और equal area A के दो rods, पर अलग moduli Y one और Y two, जो length two L की एक ही rod में जुड़े हैं।
चूँकि यह series arrangement है, दोनों rods same tension F झेलते हैं, और total stretch दोनों individual stretches का sum है।
तो reciprocal stiffnesses जुड़ती हैं, और हर rod का k उसके अपने Y times A बटा L के बराबर है। इसे starting equation लिख लीजिए।
अब combined rod को एक object मानिए: इसकी length two L, वही area A, और कोई effective modulus Y equivalent, तो इसकी stiffness है Y equivalent times A बटा two L.

substitute कीजिए और areas तथा lengths साफ़ cancel हो जाते हैं, देते हुए two over Y equivalent बराबर one over Y one plus one over Y two, जो rearrange होकर Y equivalent बराबर two Y one Y two बटा sum Y one plus Y two.
<whisper>इसे गाँठ बाँध लीजिए: answer harmonic-type combination है, Y one और Y two का simple average नहीं। arithmetic mean लिखना पूरे chapter की सबसे common गलतियों में से एक है।

board_events.text: A gas has no fixed bulk modulus: how you compress it changes its resistance. Start from $B = -V\,dP/dV$.
Since $\gamma \gt 1$, a gas always resists sudden compression more stiffly than slow compression.
This is why sound, an adiabatic wave, travels faster than Newton's isothermal estimate.

segments.text: Solids had fixed moduli. A gas is different, and this derivation shows why its bulk modulus is not a single number at all.
The picture contrasts the two cases: compress slowly and heat escapes, compress suddenly and it does not. Watch how the answer changes between them.
The reason a gas has no fixed bulk modulus is that how you compress it changes its resistance. We start from the definition, B equals minus V times d P by d V.

Compress slowly, at constant temperature, and the gas obeys P V equals a constant. Differentiate that, and minus V d P by d V comes out to just P. So the isothermal bulk modulus equals the pressure P.

Compress suddenly, with no heat exchange, and the gas obeys P V to the power gamma equals a constant. Differentiate that, and minus V d P by d V comes out to gamma P. So the adiabatic bulk modulus equals gamma times P.
Because gamma is always greater than one, a gas resists a sudden squeeze more stiffly than a slow one. The same gas, two different answers, set entirely by the process.
<curious>This is not a curiosity: it is exactly why sound, which is an adiabatic compression wave, travels faster than the isothermal estimate Newton first guessed. The gamma is the fix.
solids के moduli fixed थे। gas अलग है, और यह derivation दिखाती है कि इसका bulk modulus एक single number है ही नहीं।
picture दोनों cases का contrast करती है: धीरे compress कीजिए और heat निकल जाती है, अचानक compress कीजिए और नहीं। देखिए answer इनके बीच कैसे बदलता है।
gas का bulk modulus fixed न होने की वजह यह है कि आप उसे कैसे compress करते हैं वो resistance बदल देता है। हम definition से शुरू करते हैं, B बराबर minus V times d P by d V.
constant temperature पर धीरे compress कीजिए और gas P V बराबर constant मानता है। इसे differentiate कीजिए, और minus V d P by d V निकलता है सिर्फ़ P. तो isothermal bulk modulus pressure P के बराबर।

बिना heat exchange के अचानक compress कीजिए और gas P V to the power gamma बराबर constant मानता है। इसे differentiate कीजिए, और minus V d P by d V निकलता है gamma P. तो adiabatic bulk modulus gamma times P के बराबर।
चूँकि gamma हमेशा one से बड़ा है, gas एक अचानक squeeze को धीमे से ज़्यादा stiffly resist करता है। वही gas, दो अलग answers, पूरी तरह process से तय।
<curious>यह कोई curiosity नहीं: यही वजह है कि sound, जो एक adiabatic compression wave है, Newton के पहले-पहल अंदाज़े वाले isothermal estimate से तेज़ चलता है। gamma ही सुधार है।

board_events.text: For a uniform isotropic material, know any two of Young's, bulk, rigidity and Poisson's, and the other two are fixed.
Eliminate $\nu$ between these two relations to link Y, B and $\eta$ directly.
They all trace back to the same inter-atomic bonds, so they cannot be independent.
These relations hold only for homogeneous, isotropic materials; wood and composites need many more constants.

segments.text: Now the elegant secret of elasticity. The four constants look like four separate properties, but they are not.
The picture says it in one glance: the four constants sit at the corners, all wired together. For a uniform, isotropic material, only two of them are ever free.
Concretely, if you know any two of Young's modulus, bulk modulus, rigidity, and Poisson's ratio, the remaining two are already determined, no extra measurement needed.
The binding relation is Y equals two eta times one plus nu, which also equals three B times one minus two nu. Two expressions for the same Young's modulus.
If you eliminate Poisson's ratio nu between those two expressions, you get a clean link among the other three constants alone.
That link is nine over Y equals one over B plus three over eta. A single tidy equation connecting Young's, bulk, and rigidity moduli.
<curious>Why should nature be so economical? Because stretching, shearing, and squeezing are not separate magical properties; they all trace back to the same inter-atomic bonds from subtopic one.
One caution: these relations hold only for homogeneous, isotropic materials. Wood, fibre composites, and single crystals are anisotropic and need a whole matrix of constants, not just two.
अब elasticity का elegant राज़। चार constants चार अलग properties जैसे लगते हैं, पर हैं नहीं।
picture एक नज़र में कह देती है: चारों constants कोनों पर बैठे हैं, सब आपस में जुड़े। uniform, isotropic material के लिए इनमें से सिर्फ़ दो ही free होते हैं।
ठोस रूप में, अगर आप Young's modulus, bulk modulus, rigidity, और Poisson's ratio में से कोई दो जानते हैं, बाकी दो पहले से तय हैं, कोई extra measurement नहीं चाहिए।
binding relation है Y बराबर two eta times one plus nu, जो three B times one minus two nu के भी बराबर है। एक ही Young's modulus के दो expressions.
अगर आप उन दो expressions के बीच Poisson's ratio nu को eliminate कर दें, तो बाकी तीन constants के बीच अकेले एक साफ़ link मिलता है।
वो link है nine over Y बराबर one over B plus three over eta. एक single साफ़-सुथरी equation जो Young's, bulk, और rigidity moduli को जोड़ती है।
<curious>nature इतनी किफ़ायती क्यों? क्योंकि stretching, shearing, और squeezing अलग जादुई properties नहीं; ये सब subtopic one के उन्हीं inter-atomic bonds पर लौटते हैं।
एक चेतावनी: ये relations सिर्फ़ homogeneous, isotropic materials के लिए चलते हैं। wood, fibre composites, और single crystals anisotropic हैं और सिर्फ़ दो नहीं, constants का पूरा matrix माँगते हैं।

board_events.text: A change in length under a pull or push along one axis calls for Young's modulus Y.
A change in shape, faces sliding or twisting with volume unchanged, calls for rigidity eta.
A change in volume under all-round pressure with shape unchanged calls for bulk modulus B.
For a fluid, only B exists; for a gas, check isothermal (B=P) or adiabatic (B=gamma P).
Decide what is actually deforming, and the correct modulus is never in doubt.

segments.text: Before the numericals, a decision rule that stops you reaching for the wrong constant under exam pressure.
The picture is the whole rule at a glance: four little deformation icons, each pointing to its own modulus. Match the deformation, and you are done.
First case. Is the deformation a change in length, caused by a pull or push along a single axis? Then it is Young's modulus, Y.
Second case. Is it a change in shape, with faces sliding past each other or the object twisting, while the volume stays the same? Then it is the rigidity, eta.
Third case. Is it a change in volume under an all-around pressure, with the shape unchanged? Then it is the bulk modulus, B.

<whisper>And the special case: if the material is a fluid, a liquid or a gas, only the bulk modulus exists. For a gas, take one more step and ask whether the process is isothermal, giving B equals P, or adiabatic, giving B equals gamma P.
So the habit is simple: decide what is actually deforming first, and the correct modulus follows automatically. Never guess the modulus before naming the deformation.
numericals से पहले, एक decision rule जो exam के दबाव में आपको गलत constant उठाने से रोकती है।
picture पूरी rule एक नज़र में है: चार छोटे deformation icons, हर एक अपने modulus की ओर इशारा करता। deformation match कीजिए, और काम ख़त्म।
पहला case. क्या deformation length का change है, किसी single axis पर pull या push से? तो यह Young's modulus, Y है।
दूसरा case. क्या यह shape का change है, faces एक-दूसरे पर सरकते या object मुड़ते हुए, जबकि volume वही रहे? तो यह rigidity, eta है।
तीसरा case. क्या यह all-around pressure में volume का change है, shape बदले बिना? तो यह bulk modulus, B है।

<whisper>और special case: अगर material एक fluid है, liquid या gas, तो सिर्फ़ bulk modulus मौजूद है। gas के लिए एक कदम और लीजिए और पूछिए कि process isothermal है, देते B बराबर P, या adiabatic, देते B बराबर gamma P.
तो आदत सरल है: पहले तय कीजिए कि असल में deform क्या हो रहा है, और सही modulus अपने आप आ जाता है। deformation का नाम लेने से पहले modulus कभी मत guess कीजिए।

sections.title: The elastic-moduli formula toolkit

board_events.text: The elastic-moduli toolkit

board_events.latex: Y_{eq} = \dfrac{2Y_1 Y_2}{Y_1 + Y_2}\quad\text{(two equal rods in series)}

board_events.text: Only two of the four constants are ever independent.

segments.text: Here is the full toolkit for this subtopic on one board. Everything you need for the numericals lives here.
First, the master reinterpretation: a wire is a spring with force constant k equals Y A over L.
Then the combination rules: for series, add the reciprocals of the stiffnesses; for parallel, add the stiffnesses directly.
For the common case of two equal rods joined in series, the equivalent Young's modulus is two Y one Y two over the sum, the harmonic-type combination, never the average.
Now compressibility and its friends: k is one over B, the fractional volume change is minus delta P over B, and the fractional density change is plus delta P over B.
For a gas, remember the process sets the answer: isothermal bulk modulus is P, adiabatic is gamma P, and their ratio is exactly gamma.
And the relations that bind the constants: Y equals two eta times one plus nu, equals three B times one minus two nu, and nine over Y equals one over B plus three over eta.
<excited>One line to rule them all: out of Young's, bulk, rigidity, and Poisson's, only two are ever independent.
इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit एक board पर यहाँ है। numericals के लिए जो चाहिए सब यहीं रहता है।
पहला, master reinterpretation: एक wire एक spring है जिसका force constant k बराबर Y A बटा L है।
फिर combination rules: series के लिए stiffnesses के reciprocals जोड़िए; parallel के लिए stiffnesses सीधे जोड़िए।
series में जुड़े दो equal rods के common case के लिए, equivalent Young's modulus है two Y one Y two बटा sum, harmonic-type combination, कभी average नहीं।
अब compressibility और उसके साथी: k है one over B, fractional volume change है minus delta P बटा B, और fractional density change है plus delta P बटा B.
gas के लिए याद रखिए process ही answer तय करता है: isothermal bulk modulus P है, adiabatic gamma P, और इनका ratio ठीक gamma.
और वो relations जो constants को बाँधते हैं: Y बराबर two eta times one plus nu, बराबर three B times one minus two nu, और nine over Y बराबर one over B plus three over eta.
<excited>एक line जो सब पर राज करे: Young's, bulk, rigidity, और Poisson's में से सिर्फ़ दो ही कभी independent होते हैं।

board_events.text: Given: edge 10 cm so V = 1.0e-3 m-cubed, pressure rise 7.0e7 Pa, bulk modulus 1.4e11 Pa.
The minus sign confirms a decrease. Tiny, because copper is extremely incompressible.

segments.text: Time to use the toolkit. Start with a clean board-level bulk-modulus numerical.
The picture sets the scene: a solid copper cube squeezed by the same pressure on every one of its faces.

The data: a cube of edge ten centimetres, so its volume is one point zero times ten to the minus three cubic metres; the applied pressure rise is seven point zero times ten to the seven pascals; and the bulk modulus of copper is one point four times ten to the eleven pascals.
Rearranging the definition of bulk modulus gives the volume change: delta V equals minus delta P times V over B.

Substitute: minus, seven point zero times ten to the seven times one point zero times ten to the minus three, all over one point four times ten to the eleven, which is minus seven point zero times ten to the four over one point four times ten to the eleven.
That works out to minus five point zero times ten to the minus seven cubic metres, which is minus zero point five zero cubic centimetres.

<curious>The minus sign simply confirms the volume decreased, exactly as a squeeze should. And notice how tiny the change is: copper is extremely incompressible, so an enormous pressure barely dents its volume.

picture दृश्य तय करती है: एक solid copper cube जिसकी हर एक face पर same pressure दब रहा है।

data: दस सेंटीमीटर edge का cube, तो इसका volume है one point zero times ten to the minus three cubic metres; लगाया गया pressure rise है seven point zero times ten to the seven pascals; और copper का bulk modulus है one point four times ten to the eleven pascals.

sections.title: NEET: a gas's process-dependent bulk modulus

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: bulk modulus of a gas
Trap: students hunt for a tabulated 'bulk modulus of the gas'. For a gas, B is set by the process.
Given a diatomic gas, gamma = 1.4, at pressure 1.0e5 Pa. Find B when compressed slowly, then suddenly.
If an option gives one fixed value for a gas independent of the process, eliminate it instantly.
The whole question collapses to a single decision: is the compression slow or fast?

segments.text: Now a N E E T speed trap that rewards recall over calculation.

The trap is baked into the wording. Students go hunting for a bulk modulus of the gas as if it were a tabulated material constant, or they reach for a solid's formula. For a gas, neither works: the process sets B.

The data is minimal: a diatomic gas with gamma equal to one point four, sitting at a pressure of one point zero times ten to the five pascals. Find its bulk modulus first for slow compression, then for sudden compression.
Slow compression is isothermal, so the bulk modulus is simply the pressure: B equals P, that is one point zero times ten to the five pascals.

Sudden compression is adiabatic, so the bulk modulus is gamma times the pressure: B equals one point four times one point zero times ten to the five, which is one point four times ten to the five pascals.
<excited>And here is the exam radar: if any option offers a single fixed bulk modulus for the gas, independent of the process, eliminate it on sight. It cannot be right.
There was no real calculation here. The entire question collapses to one decision, slow or fast, and the two formulas do the rest.
अब एक N E E T speed trap जो calculation से ज़्यादा recall को इनाम देता है।

trap wording में ही पका है। students gas का bulk modulus ऐसे ढूँढते हैं मानो वो एक tabulated material constant हो, या solid का formula उठा लेते हैं। gas के लिए दोनों नहीं चलते: process ही B तय करता है।

data कम है: gamma बराबर one point four वाली एक diatomic gas, one point zero times ten to the five pascals pressure पर। इसका bulk modulus पहले slow compression के लिए, फिर sudden compression के लिए निकालिए।
slow compression isothermal है, तो bulk modulus बस pressure है: B बराबर P, यानी one point zero times ten to the five pascals.
sudden compression adiabatic है, तो bulk modulus gamma times pressure है: B बराबर one point four times one point zero times ten to the five, जो है one point four times ten to the five pascals.
<excited>और यहाँ exam radar है: अगर कोई option gas के लिए एक single fixed bulk modulus देता है, process से independent, तो उसे देखते ही हटा दीजिए। वो सही हो ही नहीं सकता।
यहाँ कोई असली calculation थी ही नहीं। पूरा सवाल एक decision पर सिमट जाता है, slow या fast, और बाकी दोनों formulas कर देते हैं।

board_events.text: Same force in series; the areas are $A_1 = \pi R^2$ and $A_2 = 4A_1$.
Same force means energy $U \propto \Delta L$, so the thin upper wire stores four times the energy of the thick one.
The weakest link does the most work and is the first to snap.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main problem that folds together the series rule and elastic energy.
The picture: two wires of the same material joined end-to-end, the upper of radius R and the lower of radius two R, with a hundred-newton load hanging below.
Two facts drive it. The wires are in series, so both carry the same force, and their areas are A one equals pi R squared for the thin wire, and A two equals four times A one for the thick one.

For the thin upper wire, delta L one is F L over A one Y. That is one hundred times one point zero, over seven point eight five times ten to the minus seven times two point zero times ten to the eleven, giving six point four times ten to the minus four metres.
The thick lower wire has four times the area, so its stretch is one quarter of the thin one: delta L two equals one point six times ten to the minus four metres.
Add them for the total elongation: eight point zero times ten to the minus four metres, that is zero point eight zero millimetres.

Now the energy twist. Because both wires carry the same force, the stored energy is proportional to the stretch. The thin wire stretches four times as much, so it stores four times the energy of the thick one.
<whisper>There is a lesson hiding in that: the weakest, thinnest link does the most work and soaks up the most energy, which is exactly why it is the first to snap.
अब एक J E E Main problem जो series rule और elastic energy को एक साथ मोड़ता है।
picture: same material की दो wires end-to-end जुड़ीं, ऊपरी radius R और निचली radius two R, नीचे hundred-newton load लटका हुआ।

पतली ऊपरी wire के लिए, delta L one है F L बटा A one Y. यानी one hundred times one point zero, बटा seven point eight five times ten to the minus seven times two point zero times ten to the eleven, देते हुए six point four times ten to the minus four metres.
मोटी निचली wire का area चार गुना है, तो इसका stretch पतली का एक-चौथाई: delta L two बराबर one point six times ten to the minus four metres.
total elongation के लिए इन्हें जोड़िए: eight point zero times ten to the minus four metres, यानी zero point eight zero millimetres.
अब energy का मोड़। चूँकि दोनों wires same force झेलती हैं, stored energy stretch के proportional है। पतली wire चार गुना खिंचती है, तो वो मोटी की चार गुना energy store करती है।
<whisper>इसमें एक सबक छिपा है: सबसे कमज़ोर, सबसे पतली कड़ी सबसे ज़्यादा काम करती है और सबसे ज़्यादा energy सोखती है, इसीलिए वही सबसे पहले टूटती है।

sections.title: JEE Advanced: relating the four constants

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: from Y and nu to B and eta
An isotropic material has Y = 1.2e11 Pa and Poisson's ratio 0.25. Use the two master relations directly.
Verify with the third relation, nine over Y equals one over B plus three over eta.
Two routes agree, confirming the material is fixed by just two constants.

segments.text: For the last worked example, a J E E Advanced check on the constant relations.

The material is homogeneous and isotropic, with Young's modulus one point two times ten to the eleven pascals and Poisson's ratio zero point two five. We are asked for the bulk and shear moduli, using the two master relations directly.

First the bulk modulus. B equals Y over three times one minus two nu. With nu of zero point two five, the bracket is one minus zero point five, so B is one point two times ten to the eleven over one point five, which is eight point zero times ten to the ten pascals.
Next the shear modulus. Eta equals Y over two times one plus nu. That is one point two times ten to the eleven over two point five, giving four point eight times ten to the ten pascals.
Now the elegant part: verify the answers are mutually consistent using the third relation, nine over Y equals one over B plus three over eta.

Compute the right side: one over B is one point two five times ten to the minus eleven, and three over eta is six point two five times ten to the minus eleven, which sum to seven point five times ten to the minus eleven.
Compute the left side: nine over one point two times ten to the eleven is also seven point five times ten to the minus eleven. The two sides match exactly.
<excited>The agreement is the whole point: two independent routes give the same number, confirming that this material is described self-consistently by just two elastic constants.
आख़िरी worked example के लिए, constant relations पर एक J E E Advanced check.

material homogeneous और isotropic है, Young's modulus one point two times ten to the eleven pascals और Poisson's ratio zero point two five के साथ। हमसे bulk और shear moduli पूछे गए हैं, दो master relations सीधे इस्तेमाल करते हुए।

पहले bulk modulus. B बराबर Y बटा three times one minus two nu. nu zero point two five के साथ, bracket है one minus zero point five, तो B है one point two times ten to the eleven बटा one point five, जो है eight point zero times ten to the ten pascals.
फिर shear modulus. eta बराबर Y बटा two times one plus nu. यानी one point two times ten to the eleven बटा two point five, देते हुए four point eight times ten to the ten pascals.
अब elegant हिस्सा: तीसरे relation से answers की आपसी consistency verify कीजिए, nine over Y बराबर one over B plus three over eta.

right side निकालिए: one over B है one point two five times ten to the minus eleven, और three over eta है six point two five times ten to the minus eleven, जिनका sum है seven point five times ten to the minus eleven.
left side निकालिए: nine बटा one point two times ten to the eleven भी seven point five times ten to the minus eleven है। दोनों sides बिलकुल match करती हैं।
<excited>यही agreement पूरा मक़सद है: दो independent routes एक ही number देते हैं, पुष्टि करते कि यह material सिर्फ़ दो elastic constants से self-consistently describe होता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and the spring-picture pro-tip

board_events.text: Pitfalls and one pro-tip
Averaging series moduli: the equivalent is 2Y1Y2/(Y1+Y2), NOT half of (Y1+Y2).
A gas has no single bulk modulus: always ask isothermal (B=P) or adiabatic (B=gamma P).
Only two of Young's, bulk, rigidity, Poisson's are independent; do not treat them as four free numbers.
The spring constant $k=YA/L$ is geometry-dependent; Young's modulus is material-only. Cutting a wire changes k, never Y.
Pro-tip: redraw any connected wires as springs with k = YA/L and use the spring rules.
That turns an unfamiliar elasticity problem into a Class 11 spring problem and dodges every average-versus-reciprocal trap.

segments.text: Let us close this subtopic by pinning down the traps that quietly cost marks.

First, the big one: never average series moduli. For rods joined end-to-end, the equivalent Young's modulus is two Y one Y two over the sum, not one half of the sum. Series means stretches add, which means reciprocals add.
Second, a gas has no single bulk modulus. Every time, ask whether the compression is isothermal, giving B equals P, or adiabatic, giving B equals gamma P. Using the wrong one is an instant error.

Third, remember only two of the four constants are independent. If a problem hands you any two of Young's, bulk, rigidity, and Poisson's, the other two are already fixed, so do not treat them as four free numbers.

Fourth, keep k and Y separate in your head. The spring constant k equals Y A over L is geometry-dependent, but Young's modulus is a property of the material alone. Cutting or rejoining a wire changes k, never Y.

<excited>And the pro-tip that ties the whole subtopic together: the moment wires are connected, redraw them as springs with k equals Y A over L, and use the series and parallel rules you already know.
That single move turns an unfamiliar elasticity problem into a Class eleven spring problem you have already mastered, and it sidesteps every average-versus-reciprocal trap in one stroke.
चलिए इस subtopic को उन traps पर उँगली रखकर बंद करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks ले जाते हैं।

पहला, बड़ा वाला: series moduli को कभी average मत कीजिए। end-to-end जुड़े rods के लिए equivalent Young's modulus है two Y one Y two बटा sum, sum का one half नहीं। series का मतलब stretches जुड़ते हैं, यानी reciprocals जुड़ते हैं।
दूसरा, gas का कोई single bulk modulus नहीं होता। हर बार पूछिए कि compression isothermal है, देते B बराबर P, या adiabatic, देते B बराबर gamma P. गलत वाला इस्तेमाल तुरंत गलती है।

तीसरा, याद रखिए चार में से सिर्फ़ दो constants independent हैं। अगर कोई problem आपको Young's, bulk, rigidity, और Poisson's में से कोई दो देती है, बाकी दो पहले से तय हैं, तो इन्हें चार free numbers मत मानिए।
चौथा, k और Y को दिमाग़ में अलग रखिए। spring constant k बराबर Y A बटा L geometry-dependent है, पर Young's modulus सिर्फ़ material की property है। wire काटना या दोबारा जोड़ना k बदलता है, Y कभी नहीं।

<excited>और वो pro-tip जो पूरे subtopic को बाँध देता है: जैसे ही wires connected हों, उन्हें k बराबर Y A बटा L वाली springs में redraw कीजिए, और वही series और parallel rules इस्तेमाल कीजिए जो आप पहले से जानते हैं।
यह एक चाल एक अनजान elasticity problem को उस Class eleven spring problem में बदल देती है जिसमें आप पहले से माहिर हैं, और एक झटके में हर average-versus-reciprocal trap से बचा देती है।

board_events.text: Pull a thick rubber band and it visibly thins: stretching one way always squeezes the perpendicular directions.
The minus sign makes $\nu$ positive, because the two strains always have opposite signs.
Rubber has $\nu \approx 0.5$ and necks a lot; cork has $\nu \approx 0$ and barely changes; metals sit near 0.2 to 0.4.
Poisson's ratio is dimensionless, with a practical range 0 to 0.5.

segments.text: In subtopic two, Poisson's ratio was the quiet constant linking the other three. Now we put it centre stage and follow it to its most useful consequence.
Look at the picture. A rod pulled along its length gets longer, but it also necks in, getting thinner across. Poisson's ratio measures exactly that trade.
You can feel it directly: stretch a thick rubber band between your hands and watch it thin. Pulling in one direction always squeezes the perpendicular directions.
We define it as nu equals minus the lateral strain over the longitudinal strain, which for a wire is minus the fractional change in radius over the fractional change in length.
Why the minus sign? Because when the length grows the radius shrinks, so the two strains carry opposite signs. The minus makes the quoted nu a clean positive number.

The values tell a story. Rubber has a Poisson's ratio near zero point five and necks dramatically; cork has a Poisson's ratio near zero and barely changes width, which is exactly why cork slides into a wine bottle without bulging; ordinary metals sit between about zero point two and zero point four.
<curious>And like strain itself, Poisson's ratio is completely dimensionless. For real materials its practical range is just zero to zero point five, a bound we are about to explain.
subtopic two में Poisson's ratio बाकी तीन को जोड़ने वाला शांत constant था। अब हम इसे केंद्र में लाते हैं और इसके सबसे useful नतीजे तक इसका पीछा करते हैं।
picture देखिए। अपनी length के साथ खींची rod लंबी होती है, पर साथ ही neck भी करती है, आर-पार पतली होती हुई। Poisson's ratio ठीक इसी सौदे को नापता है।
आप इसे सीधे महसूस कर सकते हैं: एक मोटी rubber band को हाथों के बीच खींचिए और उसे पतला होते देखिए। एक दिशा में खींचना हमेशा perpendicular directions को दबाता है।
हम इसे define करते हैं nu बराबर minus lateral strain बटा longitudinal strain, जो एक wire के लिए है minus fractional change in radius बटा fractional change in length.
minus sign क्यों? क्योंकि जब length बढ़ती है radius घटता है, तो दोनों strains के signs उल्टे होते हैं। minus quoted nu को एक साफ़ positive number बना देता है।

values एक कहानी कहती हैं। rubber का Poisson's ratio zero point five के पास है और वो नाटकीय रूप से neck करता है; cork का zero के पास है और वो चौड़ाई में मुश्किल से बदलता है, इसीलिए cork wine bottle में बिना उभरे सरक जाता है; आम metals लगभग zero point two से zero point four के बीच रहते हैं।
<curious>और strain की तरह, Poisson's ratio पूरी तरह dimensionless है। real materials के लिए इसका practical range बस zero से zero point five है, एक bound जिसे हम अभी समझाने वाले हैं।

<text x="360" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">volume constant</text>
<text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">(incompressible)</text>

board_events.text: Stretching lengthens the rod (volume wants to grow) but thins it (volume wants to shrink). Which wins?
If $\nu \lt 0.5$ the lengthening wins and volume grows; if $\nu = 0.5$ the two exactly cancel and volume stays constant.
A value above 0.5 would shrink the volume on stretching, which inter-atomic forces forbid.
That is the deep reason $\nu$ cannot exceed 0.5 for ordinary materials.

segments.text: Here is the question that makes Poisson's ratio genuinely interesting, and its answer is the payoff of the whole first half of this subtopic.
The picture frames it. When you stretch a wire it gets longer, which wants to add volume, but it also gets thinner, which wants to remove volume. The winner is not obvious.
So does the total volume go up, down, or stay put? The competition is decided entirely by Poisson's ratio.
The result is compact: the fractional volume change equals one minus two nu, times the longitudinal strain. Everything hangs on that bracket.

Read it off. If nu is less than zero point five, the bracket is positive, the lengthening wins, and the volume grows slightly on stretching. If nu equals exactly zero point five, the bracket is zero, the thinning perfectly cancels the lengthening, and the volume stays constant: the material is incompressible.
<whisper>Now the forbidden zone. A Poisson's ratio above zero point five would make the bracket negative, meaning stretching a body shrinks its volume. Inter-atomic forces simply do not permit that.
So this one relation explains the upper bound we quoted earlier: for ordinary materials, Poisson's ratio can never exceed zero point five.
यहाँ वो सवाल है जो Poisson's ratio को सचमुच दिलचस्प बनाता है, और इसका जवाब इस subtopic के पूरे पहले भाग का payoff है।
picture इसे फ्रेम करती है। जब आप wire खींचते हैं वो लंबी होती है, जो volume जोड़ना चाहती है, पर वो पतली भी होती है, जो volume हटाना चाहती है। जीतने वाला साफ़ नहीं है।
तो total volume ऊपर जाता है, नीचे, या वहीं रहता है? यह मुक़ाबला पूरी तरह Poisson's ratio से तय होता है।
result compact है: fractional volume change बराबर one minus two nu, times longitudinal strain. सब कुछ उस bracket पर टिका है।

इसे पढ़िए। अगर nu, zero point five से कम है, bracket positive है, lengthening जीतती है, और stretching पर volume थोड़ा बढ़ता है। अगर nu ठीक zero point five है, bracket zero है, thinning lengthening को बिलकुल cancel कर देती है, और volume constant रहता है: material incompressible है।
<whisper>अब forbidden zone. zero point five से ऊपर का Poisson's ratio bracket को negative बना देता, यानी body को खींचना उसका volume घटा देता। inter-atomic forces इसकी इजाज़त ही नहीं देतीं।
तो यही एक relation उस upper bound को समझाता है जो हमने पहले बताया था: आम materials के लिए Poisson's ratio कभी zero point five से ज़्यादा नहीं हो सकता।

board_events.text: For a cylinder the volume is $V = \pi r^{2} L$; taking logs turns the product into a sum.

board_events.latex: \ln V = \ln \pi + 2\ln r + \ln L \;\Rightarrow\; \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 2\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} + \dfrac{\Delta L}{L}

board_events.text: Now bring in Poisson's ratio: the radial strain is $\Delta r/r = -\nu\,\Delta L/L$.
Read off the physics: nu = 0.5 gives no volume change; nu below 0.5 grows the volume.

segments.text: Let us actually derive that volume relation, because the technique, differentiating a logarithm, is worth owning.
Picture a cylindrical bar. Its volume is pi times radius squared times length, and when we stretch it, both the radius and the length change a little.
The clean route for a product is to take the logarithm first. That converts the product V equals pi r squared L into a simple sum of logarithms.
Differentiating the log turns each term into a fractional change, giving the fractional volume change equals two times the fractional radius change plus the fractional length change.
Now the physics enters through Poisson's ratio. By definition the radial strain is minus nu times the longitudinal strain, because the radius shrinks as the length grows.
Substitute that in. The two times minus nu, plus one, collapses to one minus two nu, and we recover the fractional volume change equals one minus two nu times the longitudinal strain.

<curious>And the physics falls straight out of that single line: set nu to zero point five and the volume change is exactly zero, incompressible; keep nu below zero point five and the volume grows on stretching.
चलिए उस volume relation को सचमुच derive करते हैं, क्योंकि तकनीक, एक logarithm को differentiate करना, अपनाने लायक है।
एक cylindrical bar की कल्पना कीजिए। इसका volume है pi times radius squared times length, और जब हम इसे खींचते हैं, radius और length दोनों थोड़ा बदलते हैं।
product के लिए साफ़ रास्ता है पहले logarithm लेना। यह product V बराबर pi r squared L को logarithms के एक simple sum में बदल देता है।
log को differentiate करना हर term को एक fractional change बना देता है, देते हुए fractional volume change बराबर two times fractional radius change plus fractional length change.
अब physics Poisson's ratio के ज़रिए आती है। definition से radial strain है minus nu times longitudinal strain, क्योंकि length बढ़ने पर radius घटता है।
इसे substitute कीजिए। two times minus nu, plus one, सिमटकर one minus two nu हो जाता है, और हमें वापस मिलता है fractional volume change बराबर one minus two nu times longitudinal strain.
<curious>और physics उसी एक line से सीधे निकलती है: nu को zero point five रखिए और volume change ठीक zero, incompressible; nu को zero point five से नीचे रखिए और stretching पर volume बढ़ता है।
