board_events.text: A bow, a catapult, a trampoline: each takes in work as it deforms and pays it back on release.
A stretched wire is the same in miniature; the work goes into elastic potential energy.
The force is NOT constant: it grows from zero to F as the wire stretches.
So the stored energy uses the average force, one-half F, not the full F.

segments.text: Now the second half of this subtopic: every deformation quietly banks energy, and understanding why is what separates a careful student from a careless one.
The picture is the whole idea: plot force against extension and the energy stored is the triangular area underneath.
You already know this in your bones. Pull back the string of a bow, load a catapult, jump on a trampoline: each takes in work as it deforms and pays that work back the moment it recovers.

A stretched wire is exactly the same idea in miniature. The work you do against the inter-atomic springs does not vanish; it is stored as elastic potential energy, ready to be released the instant the load comes off.
<curious>But here is the subtlety that trips people up. The stretching force is not constant. It starts at zero on an unstretched wire and grows steadily to its final value F as the wire extends.
Because the force builds up linearly, the work is done by the average force, which is one half of F, not the full F.
So the stored energy is one half F times the elongation. That factor of one half is the whole punchline, and the next section proves it properly.
अब इस subtopic का दूसरा भाग: हर deformation चुपचाप energy जमा करता है, और यह समझना कि क्यों, एक सावधान student को लापरवाह से अलग करता है।
picture ही पूरा idea है: force को extension के सामने plot कीजिए और stored energy नीचे का triangular area है।
आप इसे अपनी हड्डियों में जानते हैं। धनुष की डोर खींचिए, गुलेल load कीजिए, trampoline पर कूदिए: हर एक deform होते हुए work लेता है और recover करते ही वो work वापस दे देता है।
एक stretched wire ठीक वही idea छोटे रूप में है। inter-atomic springs के खिलाफ़ किया आपका work ग़ायब नहीं होता; वो elastic potential energy के रूप में जमा होता है, load हटते ही release होने को तैयार।
<curious>पर यहाँ वो बारीकी है जो लोगों को गिराती है। stretching force constant नहीं है। यह unstretched wire पर zero से शुरू होती है और wire के खिंचते-खिंचते steadily अपने final value F तक बढ़ती है।
चूँकि force linearly बढ़ती है, work average force से होता है, जो F का one half है, पूरा F नहीं।
तो stored energy है one half F times elongation. वो one half factor ही पूरा punchline है, और अगला section इसे ठीक से prove करता है।

board_events.text: At extension $l$ the holding force is $F(l) = (YA/L)\,l$; a further $dl$ needs work $F(l)\,dl$.
Since the final force is $F = (YA/L)\Delta L$, this is simply $U = \tfrac{1}{2}F\,\Delta L$.
The one-half is the average force at work, not the full F.

segments.text: Let us prove the one half properly, and get the energy density as a bonus.
The stress-strain triangle in the picture is where we are heading: its area will turn out to be the energy per unit volume.

Suppose the wire has already been stretched by some amount l. From subtopic two, the force needed to hold it there is Y A over L, times l. To stretch it a tiny bit further by d l costs work F of l times d l.
Because the force grows from zero to its final value, we integrate that from zero to the final elongation. The integral of Y A over L times l gives one half Y A over L, times the elongation squared.
Now recognise the final force is Y A over L times delta L, and the whole expression collapses neatly to U equals one half F times delta L. The one half is proven, not assumed.

Divide the energy by the volume A L and regroup, and you get the energy density: one half sigma epsilon, which also equals one half Y epsilon squared, and sigma squared over two Y. Three equivalent forms.
<whisper>And keep the meaning in view: that persistent one half is nothing mysterious. It is simply the average force doing the work, from zero up to F, not the full F.
चलिए one half को ठीक से prove करते हैं, और bonus में energy density पा लेते हैं।
picture में stress-strain triangle ही वो जगह है जहाँ हम जा रहे हैं: इसका area energy per unit volume निकलेगा।
मान लीजिए wire पहले से किसी amount l खिंची है। subtopic two से, इसे वहाँ रोकने के लिए ज़रूरी force है Y A बटा L, times l. इसे d l जितना और खींचने पर work लगता है F of l times d l.
चूँकि force zero से अपने final value तक बढ़ती है, हम इसे zero से final elongation तक integrate करते हैं। Y A बटा L times l का integral देता है one half Y A बटा L, times elongation squared.
अब पहचानिए कि final force है Y A बटा L times delta L, और पूरा expression साफ़ सिमटकर U बराबर one half F times delta L हो जाता है। one half prove हुआ, माना नहीं गया।
energy को volume A L से divide करके regroup कीजिए, और मिलती है energy density: one half sigma epsilon, जो one half Y epsilon squared, और sigma squared बटा two Y के भी बराबर है। तीन equivalent रूप।
<whisper>और मतलब नज़र में रखिए: वो बार-बार आता one half कोई रहस्य नहीं। यह बस average force है जो work कर रही है, zero से F तक, पूरा F नहीं।

board_events.text: Because $u = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma\varepsilon$ and the graph plots $\sigma$ against $\varepsilon$, the area under the curve is the energy per unit volume.
It is energy DENSITY, not total energy: multiply by volume for the total.
Watch the axes: a force-extension area gives total energy directly; a stress-strain area gives density.
This area idea returns for resilience and toughness in the very next subtopic.
To any point on the curve, the shaded area is the energy stored per cubic metre up to that strain.

segments.text: One more reading skill closes the subtopic, and it is a favourite of examiners: pulling energy straight off the graph.
The picture shows the move: shade the area under the stress-strain curve, and that shaded region is the elastic energy per unit volume.

The reason is exactly the energy density we just derived. Since u is one half sigma epsilon, and the graph plots stress on the vertical against strain on the horizontal, the area under the curve is that product, the energy per unit volume.
<whisper>But hold the crucial caveat: this area is energy density, not total energy. To get the total energy you must multiply by the volume of the specimen.

So watch which graph you are handed. The area under a force-extension curve gives the total energy directly, but the area under a stress-strain curve gives energy per unit volume. Mixing these up is a classic slip.
Keep this idea warm, because it comes straight back in the next subtopic, where the area to yield is called resilience and the total area to fracture is called toughness.
For now, the rule is simple: shade under the curve up to any point, and you have read off the energy stored per cubic metre right up to that strain.
एक और reading skill subtopic को बंद करती है, और यह examiners की पसंदीदा है: energy को सीधे graph से खींच लेना।
picture चाल दिखाती है: stress-strain curve के नीचे का area shade कीजिए, और वो shaded region elastic energy per unit volume है।

वजह ठीक वही energy density है जो हमने अभी derive की। चूँकि u है one half sigma epsilon, और graph vertical पर stress को horizontal पर strain के सामने plot करता है, curve के नीचे का area वही product है, energy per unit volume.
<whisper>पर ज़रूरी caveat थामे रखिए: यह area energy density है, total energy नहीं। total energy पाने के लिए आपको specimen के volume से multiply करना होगा।

तो ध्यान दीजिए आपको कौन सा graph दिया गया है। force-extension curve के नीचे का area सीधे total energy देता है, पर stress-strain curve के नीचे का area energy per unit volume देता है। इन्हें आपस में मिलाना एक classic गलती है।
इस idea को गरम रखिए, क्योंकि यह अगले ही subtopic में लौटता है, जहाँ yield तक का area resilience कहलाता है और fracture तक का total area toughness.
फ़िलहाल, rule सरल है: curve के नीचे किसी भी point तक shade कीजिए, और आपने उस strain तक stored energy per cubic metre पढ़ ली।

sections.title: The Poisson and elastic-energy toolkit

board_events.text: Poisson and energy toolkit
Every one-half here comes from the average force building up from zero.

segments.text: Here is the full toolkit for this subtopic on one board, the reference for every numerical ahead.
First, Poisson's ratio: minus the lateral strain over the longitudinal strain, dimensionless, with the practical range zero to zero point five.
Second, the volume relation: the fractional volume change equals one minus two nu, times the longitudinal strain.
Third, the elastic energy in three equivalent forms: one half F times the elongation, one half stress times strain times the volume, and one half Y A over L, times elongation squared.
Fourth, the energy density: one half sigma epsilon, which also equals one half Y epsilon squared, and sigma squared over two Y.
Fifth, the loading contrast: load gradually and the work all becomes stored energy with no heat; load suddenly and the maximum stretch is twice the static value.
<excited>And the one line to remember them by: every single one half on this board comes from the same fact, the force building up from zero, so the average is F over two.
इस subtopic का पूरा toolkit एक board पर यहाँ है, आगे के हर numerical का reference.
पहला, Poisson's ratio: minus lateral strain बटा longitudinal strain, dimensionless, practical range zero से zero point five के साथ।
दूसरा, volume relation: fractional volume change बराबर one minus two nu, times longitudinal strain.
तीसरा, elastic energy तीन equivalent रूपों में: one half F times elongation, one half stress times strain times volume, और one half Y A बटा L, times elongation squared.
चौथा, energy density: one half sigma epsilon, जो one half Y epsilon squared, और sigma squared बटा two Y के भी बराबर है।
पाँचवाँ, loading का contrast: gradually load कीजिए और पूरा work stored energy बन जाता है बिना heat; suddenly load कीजिए और maximum stretch static value का दुगना होता है।
<excited>और इन्हें याद रखने वाली एक line: इस board का हर एक one half उसी एक fact से आता है, force का zero से बढ़ना, तो average है F बटा two.

sections.title: CBSE: energy stored in a steel wire

board_events.text: CBSE: energy stored in a stretched steel wire
Given: L = 2.0 m, A = 1.0e-6 m-squared, elongation 1.0e-3 m, Y = 2.0e11 Pa. First find the force.
Energy density is independent of how much wire you have.

segments.text: Let us cash in the energy formulas on a clean board-level problem.

The data: a steel wire two point zero metres long, cross-section one times ten to the minus six square metres, stretched by one times ten to the minus three metres, with Young's modulus two times ten to the eleven pascals. As always, start by finding the force.

The force is Y A delta L over L. Multiplying through gives two times ten to the eleven, times one times ten to the minus six, times one times ten to the minus three, all over two point zero, which is one hundred newtons.
Now the stored energy. U is one half F times delta L, that is one half of one hundred times one times ten to the minus three, which comes out to zero point zero five joules.

For the energy density, first the volume: area times length is two times ten to the minus six cubic metres. Divide the energy by that and you get two point five times ten to the four joules per cubic metre.

<curious>Always cross-check by the other route. u equals one half sigma epsilon; with stress ten to the eight and strain five times ten to the minus four, that is also two point five times ten to the four joules per cubic metre. The two agree.
And note the concept the number teaches: energy density is a property of the material and the strain, independent of how much wire you happen to have.
चलिए energy formulas को एक साफ़ board-level problem पर भुनाते हैं।

data: steel wire two point zero metres लंबी, cross-section one times ten to the minus six square metres, one times ten to the minus three metres खिंची, Young's modulus two times ten to the eleven pascals के साथ। हमेशा की तरह, force निकालकर शुरू कीजिए।

force है Y A delta L बटा L. गुणा करने पर मिलता है two times ten to the eleven, times one times ten to the minus six, times one times ten to the minus three, सब बटा two point zero, जो है one hundred newtons.
अब stored energy. U है one half F times delta L, यानी one half of one hundred times one times ten to the minus three, जो निकलता है zero point zero five joules.

energy density के लिए पहले volume: area times length है two times ten to the minus six cubic metres. energy को इससे divide कीजिए और मिलता है two point five times ten to the four joules per cubic metre.

<curious>हमेशा दूसरे रास्ते से cross-check कीजिए। u बराबर one half sigma epsilon; stress ten to the eight और strain five times ten to the minus four के साथ, यह भी two point five times ten to the four joules per cubic metre है। दोनों मिलते हैं।
और वो concept देखिए जो यह number सिखाता है: energy density material और strain की property है, इस बात से independent कि आपके पास कितनी wire है।

sections.title: NEET: area under the curve is a density

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: area under the curve
Trap: students read the area under a stress-strain graph as the total energy. It is energy per unit volume.
Given: area under the curve 8e4 J per cubic metre, wire volume 5e-6 m-cubed.
If an option gives 8e4 J, that is the area misread as total energy: the planted trap.
The unit, joules per cubic metre on the area, is your tell that it is a density.
Multiply by volume and the units resolve cleanly to joules.

segments.text: Here is a N E E T trap that lives entirely in a misread unit.
The bait is familiar: students see the phrase area under the stress-strain curve and write it down as the total energy. It is not; it is the energy per unit volume.
The data is deliberately spare: the area under the curve is eight times ten to the four joules per cubic metre, and the wire has a volume of five times ten to the minus six cubic metres.
So the total energy is just the density times the volume: eight times ten to the four, times five times ten to the minus six, which is zero point four joules.
<excited>Now spot the plant. If an option offers eight times ten to the four joules, that is exactly the area misread as a total energy. Eliminate it.
The tell is right there in the unit. The area carries joules per cubic metre, and per cubic metre screams density, not total.
Multiply by the volume and the cubic metres cancel, leaving clean joules, the honest total energy.
यहाँ एक N E E T trap है जो पूरी तरह एक misread unit में बसता है।
चारा जाना-पहचाना है: students area under the stress-strain curve वाक्यांश देखते हैं और उसे total energy लिख देते हैं। यह वो नहीं है; यह energy per unit volume है।
data जानबूझकर कम है: curve के नीचे का area है eight times ten to the four joules per cubic metre, और wire का volume है five times ten to the minus six cubic metres.
तो total energy बस density times volume है: eight times ten to the four, times five times ten to the minus six, जो है zero point four joules.
<excited>अब plant पहचानिए। अगर कोई option eight times ten to the four joules देता है, वो ठीक area को total energy पढ़ लेना है। उसे हटा दीजिए।
tell unit में ही है। area joules per cubic metre रखता है, और per cubic metre density चिल्लाता है, total नहीं।
volume से multiply कीजिए और cubic metres cancel हो जाते हैं, पीछे साफ़ joules छोड़ते हुए, ईमानदार total energy.

segments.text: This J E E Main problem chains all three ideas of the subtopic in one clean sequence.
The picture lays out the plan: one applied tensile stress, and from it we read off the longitudinal strain, then the lateral strain, then the volume change.
The data: a wire of Young's modulus one point two times ten to the eleven pascals, Poisson's ratio zero point three zero, carrying a tensile stress of one point two times ten to the eight pascals.

First, the longitudinal strain from Young's modulus: epsilon is stress over Y, that is one point two times ten to the eight over one point two times ten to the eleven, which is one point zero times ten to the minus three.

Next, the lateral strain from Poisson's ratio: minus nu times epsilon, that is minus zero point three zero times one point zero times ten to the minus three, giving minus three point zero times ten to the minus four. The diameter shrinks.

Finally the volume change: one minus two nu, times epsilon. The bracket is one minus zero point six, so it is zero point four times one point zero times ten to the minus three, which is four point zero times ten to the minus four.
<curious>Read the sign: the volume increases, exactly because nu is under zero point five. In everyday terms, the wire swells by about zero point zero four percent even as it thins.

फिर, Poisson's ratio से lateral strain: minus nu times epsilon, यानी minus zero point three zero times one point zero times ten to the minus three, देते हुए minus three point zero times ten to the minus four. diameter सिकुड़ता है।

आख़िर में volume change: one minus two nu, times epsilon. bracket है one minus zero point six, तो यह zero point four times one point zero times ten to the minus three, जो है four point zero times ten to the minus four.
<curious>sign पढ़िए: volume बढ़ता है, ठीक इसलिए कि nu zero point five से नीचे है। रोज़मर्रा की भाषा में, wire पतली होते हुए भी लगभग zero point zero four percent फूल जाती है।

board_events.text: Released from the just-taut position, at maximum elongation the kinetic energy is zero, so lost gravitational PE equals stored elastic energy.
The static (gradual) elongation is $x_{st} = mgL/(YA)$, so $x_{max} = 2\,x_{st}$.
The full weight acts through the whole descent; the overshoot doubles the stretch and half the work turns to heat.

segments.text: The J E E Advanced closer is the energy-partition problem, where suddenly dropping a load stretches a wire to twice the gentle value.
The picture tells the story: a block hangs from a wire that is just taut, then it is released. It falls, stretching the wire, until it momentarily stops at the maximum elongation.
At that lowest point the kinetic energy is zero, just as it was at the top. So over the whole fall, the loss in gravitational potential energy equals the elastic energy stored in the wire.
Write that balance: m g x max equals one half Y A over L, times x max squared. Cancel one factor of x max and the maximum elongation comes out to two m g L over Y A.
Now compare with the static case. Loaded gradually, the elongation would be m g L over Y A. So the sudden maximum is exactly twice the static elongation.

Put in the numbers. The static stretch is forty over two times ten to the five, which is two point zero times ten to the minus four metres, so the sudden maximum is four point zero times ten to the minus four metres, or zero point four zero millimetres.

<whisper>And here is the physics of the doubling: applied suddenly, the full weight acts through the entire descent, but the wire can only store half of that work at the equilibrium point. The mismatch shows up as kinetic energy, which overshoots and doubles the stretch, and half the input work ends up as heat.
J E E Advanced closer है energy-partition problem, जहाँ अचानक load गिराना एक wire को gentle value के दुगने तक खींच देता है।
picture कहानी कहती है: एक block एक just-taut wire से लटका है, फिर उसे release किया जाता है। वो गिरता है, wire को खींचते हुए, जब तक एक पल के लिए maximum elongation पर रुक न जाए।
उस सबसे नीचे point पर kinetic energy zero है, ठीक जैसे ऊपर थी। तो पूरे गिरने में, gravitational potential energy का loss wire में stored elastic energy के बराबर है।
वो balance लिखिए: m g x max बराबर one half Y A बटा L, times x max squared. x max का एक factor cancel कीजिए और maximum elongation निकलता है two m g L बटा Y A.
अब static case से तुलना कीजिए। gradually load करने पर elongation होता m g L बटा Y A. तो sudden maximum ठीक static elongation का दुगना है।

numbers रखिए। static stretch है forty बटा two times ten to the five, जो है two point zero times ten to the minus four metres, तो sudden maximum है four point zero times ten to the minus four metres, यानी zero point four zero millimetres.

<whisper>और यहाँ doubling की physics है: अचानक लगाने पर, पूरा weight पूरे descent में act करता है, पर wire equilibrium point पर उस work का सिर्फ़ आधा store कर सकती है। यह mismatch kinetic energy बनकर दिखता है, जो overshoot करके stretch दुगना कर देता है, और input work का आधा heat बन जाता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and the sudden-loading pro-tip

board_events.text: Pitfalls and one pro-tip
Do not drop the one-half: elastic energy is half F times elongation, because the force builds from zero.
Area under a stress-strain curve is energy per unit volume; multiply by volume for the total.
Volume is conserved only if nu is 0.5; for metals near 0.3, stretching genuinely grows the volume.
Poisson's ratio is quoted positive and can never exceed 0.5 for real materials.
Pro-tip: for sudden loading, skip the algebra and use $x_{max} = 2x_{static}$.
Recognising it turns a full energy-conservation derivation into a one-line answer.

segments.text: Let us close with the traps this subtopic plants most often.

First and most costly: never drop the one half. Elastic energy is one half F times the elongation, because the force builds up from zero, so the average force is F over two. Writing the full F doubles your answer.

Second, keep total energy and energy density apart. The area under a stress-strain curve is energy per unit volume; you must multiply by the volume to get the total. Only a force-extension curve gives total energy directly.

Third, do not assume volume is conserved when stretching. It is fixed only if Poisson's ratio is exactly zero point five. For a typical metal near zero point three, stretching genuinely increases the volume.
Fourth, mind the sign and range of Poisson's ratio. By convention it is quoted as a positive number, and for real materials it can never exceed zero point five.
<excited>And the pro-tip that saves the most time: for any sudden-loading problem, skip the full energy-conservation algebra and just write x max equals two x static.
A suddenly dropped load always stretches a wire to twice its gentle-loading elongation, so recognising it on sight turns a whole derivation into a single line.
चलिए उन traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो यह subtopic सबसे ज़्यादा बोता है।
पहला और सबसे महँगा: one half कभी मत गिराइए। elastic energy है one half F times elongation, क्योंकि force zero से बढ़ती है, तो average force F बटा two है। पूरा F लिखना आपका answer दुगना कर देता है।

दूसरा, total energy और energy density को अलग रखिए। stress-strain curve के नीचे का area energy per unit volume है; total पाने के लिए आपको volume से multiply करना होगा। सिर्फ़ force-extension curve सीधे total energy देता है।
तीसरा, खींचते समय volume conserved मान मत लीजिए। यह तभी fixed है जब Poisson's ratio ठीक zero point five हो। zero point three के पास वाले typical metal के लिए, stretching सचमुच volume बढ़ाती है।
चौथा, Poisson's ratio के sign और range का ध्यान रखिए। परंपरा से इसे positive number के रूप में quote किया जाता है, और real materials के लिए यह कभी zero point five से ज़्यादा नहीं हो सकता।
<excited>और वो pro-tip जो सबसे ज़्यादा समय बचाता है: किसी भी sudden-loading problem के लिए, पूरी energy-conservation algebra छोड़िए और बस x max बराबर two x static लिखिए।
अचानक गिराया load हमेशा wire को उसके gentle-loading elongation के दुगने तक खींचता है, तो इसे देखते ही पहचानना एक पूरी derivation को एक ही line बना देता है।

board_events.text: Up to the yield point a solid stretches and springs back faithfully, just like a spring.
Push past it and something irreversible happens: it keeps stretching with barely any extra force.
Release it now and it does NOT return to its original shape; it carries a permanent set.
On the graph, the unloading line runs parallel to the elastic line but ends short of the origin.
That residual strain, the permanent set, is the defining feature of yielding.

segments.text: In subtopic one you learned to name the landmarks on the stress-strain curve. This subtopic asks a sharper question: what actually happens at the moment a material stops behaving like a spring?
Look at the picture. The green stretch on the left is elastic, but once we push into the orange region and then let go, the wire does not retrace its path back to the origin.
Up to the yield point, every solid behaves like the springs of the last three subtopics: stretch it, and it springs back faithfully.
But push past that point and something irreversible happens. The material gives. It keeps stretching with barely any extra force, flowing rather than resisting.
<whisper>And here is the crucial part: release it now, and it does not return to its original shape. It carries a permanent set, a lasting deformation that will never come out.
You can see it on the graph. When you unload from the plastic region, the line comes down parallel to the original elastic line, but it lands short of the origin, at a non-zero strain.
That leftover strain, the permanent set, is the defining signature of yielding. Everything else in this subtopic is about what different materials do once they cross that line.
subtopic one में आपने stress-strain curve के landmarks के नाम सीखे। यह subtopic एक तेज़ सवाल पूछता है: जिस पल material spring की तरह behave करना बंद करता है, असल में तब होता क्या है?
picture देखिए। बाईं ओर green stretch elastic है, पर एक बार हम orange region में धकेलकर छोड़ देते हैं, wire अपने रास्ते से वापस origin तक नहीं लौटती।
yield point तक, हर solid पिछले तीन subtopics की springs की तरह behave करता है: खींचिए, और वो faithfully वापस आ जाता है।
पर उस point के पार धकेलिए और कुछ irreversible हो जाता है। material give कर देता है। यह बहुत थोड़े extra force पर खिंचता रहता है, resist करने के बजाय flow करता हुआ।
<whisper>और यहाँ अहम हिस्सा है: अब इसे छोड़िए, और यह अपनी original shape में नहीं लौटता। यह एक permanent set रखता है, एक स्थायी deformation जो कभी नहीं निकलेगा।
आप इसे graph पर देख सकते हैं। जब आप plastic region से unload करते हैं, line मूल elastic line के parallel नीचे आती है, पर origin से पहले, एक non-zero strain पर रुक जाती है।
वो बचा हुआ strain, permanent set, yielding का पहचान-चिह्न है। इस subtopic का बाक़ी सब इसी बारे में है कि उस line को पार करते ही अलग-अलग materials क्या करते हैं।

board_events.text: Ductile materials (copper, gold, mild steel) have a long plastic region and can be drawn into thin wires.
Malleable materials (gold, silver, aluminium, lead) yield under compression and can be hammered into sheets.
Ductility lives in tension (wires); malleability lives in compression (sheets).
Brittle materials (glass, cast iron, ceramic) snap clean, with almost no plastic region.
Most ductile metals are also malleable, but the two ideas are genuinely distinct.

segments.text: What a material does after it yields is its personality, and it sorts materials into three families. The picture shows all three curves at once.
Study the shapes: the ductile curve has a long gentle plateau and a big area, the brittle curve snaps off early, and the elastomer curve is bent from the very start.

First, ductile materials, like copper, gold, and mild steel. They have a long, generous plastic region between yielding and fracture, so they can be drawn out into thin wires. That is literally what ductility means.

Second, malleable materials, like gold, silver, aluminium, and lead. They yield easily under compression and can be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without cracking. Gold leaf on a temple dome and kitchen foil are malleability in action.
<curious>Keep the two straight with one line: ductility lives in tension, being pulled into wires, while malleability lives in compression, being beaten into sheets.
Third, brittle materials, like glass, cast iron, and ceramic. They have almost no plastic region and snap clean, going straight from fine to in pieces very soon after the elastic limit.
One nuance worth carrying: most ductile metals happen to be malleable too, but the two ideas are genuinely distinct, one about pulling, the other about hammering.
yield करने के बाद material जो करता है वही उसकी personality है, और यह materials को तीन families में छाँटती है। picture तीनों curves एक साथ दिखाती है।
shapes ध्यान से देखिए: ductile curve का लंबा gentle plateau और बड़ा area है, brittle curve जल्दी snap हो जाती है, और elastomer curve शुरू से ही मुड़ी हुई है।

पहला, ductile materials, जैसे copper, gold, और mild steel. इनका yielding और fracture के बीच लंबा, उदार plastic region होता है, तो इन्हें पतली wires में खींचा जा सकता है। ductility का शाब्दिक मतलब यही है।

दूसरा, malleable materials, जैसे gold, silver, aluminium, और lead. ये compression में आसानी से yield करते हैं और बिना टूटे पतली sheets में हथौड़े से पीटे या roll किए जा सकते हैं। मंदिर के गुंबद का gold leaf और रसोई की foil malleability का काम है।
<curious>दोनों को एक line से अलग रखिए: ductility tension में बसती है, wires में खींचे जाना, जबकि malleability compression में बसती है, sheets में पीटा जाना।
तीसरा, brittle materials, जैसे glass, cast iron, और ceramic. इनका plastic region लगभग नहीं होता और ये साफ़ snap हो जाते हैं, elastic limit के तुरंत बाद fine से सीधे टुकड़ों में।
एक बारीकी साथ रखने लायक: ज़्यादातर ductile metals malleable भी होते हैं, पर दोनों ideas सचमुच अलग हैं, एक खींचने की, दूसरी हथौड़े की।

board_events.text: Is rubber more elastic than steel? By the modulus definition, steel wins: for a given strain it develops far larger stress.
Rubber is an elastomer: it endures huge recoverable strains with essentially no proportional region.
Loading and unloading trace different curves; the enclosed loop is elastic hysteresis.
The loop area is energy quietly converted to heat on every cycle.
This is exactly why rubber is chosen for tyres and shock absorbers: it eats vibration instead of bouncing it back.

segments.text: There is a famous puzzle lurking here: is rubber more elastic than steel? The answer depends entirely on which definition you use.
The picture holds the key idea for rubber: its loading path and its unloading path are different curves, and between them sits an enclosed loop.

In everyday language rubber wins, since it stretches enormously and pings right back. But by the physics definition, elasticity is the restoring stress per unit strain, and for a given strain steel develops vastly larger internal stress, so steel is the more elastic.

Rubber belongs to a special class called elastomers. An elastomer endures huge strains elastically, several times its length, but has essentially no proportional region, so Hooke's law never really applies to it.
<curious>And crucially, an elastomer does not retrace its path on unloading. The loading and unloading curves enclose a loop, and that loop is called elastic hysteresis.
The area inside that loop is not free. It is energy quietly converted to heat on every single loading cycle, which is also why a much-flexed rubber band feels warm.
This is the whole reason rubber is chosen for vehicle tyres and shock absorbers. It eats vibration energy and turns it to heat, rather than bouncing it straight back at you.
यहाँ एक मशहूर पहेली छिपी है: क्या rubber steel से ज़्यादा elastic है? जवाब पूरी तरह इस पर निर्भर है कि आप कौन सी definition इस्तेमाल करते हैं।
picture rubber का मुख्य idea थामे है: इसका loading path और unloading path अलग curves हैं, और इनके बीच एक enclosed loop बैठा है।

रोज़मर्रा की भाषा में rubber जीतता है, क्योंकि वो बहुत खिंचता है और वापस उछल आता है। पर physics की definition से, elasticity है restoring stress per unit strain, और किसी दिए strain पर steel कहीं बड़ा internal stress पैदा करता है, तो steel ज़्यादा elastic है।

rubber एक ख़ास वर्ग का है जिसे elastomers कहते हैं। एक elastomer भारी strains को elastically झेलता है, अपनी length का कई गुना, पर इसका proportional region लगभग नहीं होता, तो Hooke's law इस पर कभी सचमुच लागू नहीं होता।
<curious>और अहम बात, एक elastomer unloading पर अपने रास्ते को दोबारा नहीं दोहराता। loading और unloading curves एक loop घेरती हैं, और उस loop को elastic hysteresis कहते हैं।
उस loop के अंदर का area मुफ़्त नहीं है। यह हर एक loading cycle पर चुपचाप heat में बदली energy है, इसीलिए बहुत मोड़ी गई rubber band गरम महसूस होती है।
यही पूरी वजह है कि rubber vehicle tyres और shock absorbers के लिए चुना जाता है। यह vibration energy खा जाता है और heat में बदल देता है, बजाय इसके कि उसे सीधे आप पर वापस उछाल दे।

board_events.text: Heat: many brittle metals turn ductile when hot, which is why a blacksmith heats iron before hammering.
Rate of loading: sudden shocks make even ductile metals behave brittlely.
Repeated cycling causes elastic fatigue: a part can fail well below its normal breaking stress.
This is why aircraft parts and railway axles are retired on a schedule, not just when they look worn.
So these labels are material properties, but they are not frozen; conditions move them.

segments.text: One more concept before the numbers: these family labels are not carved in stone. Three conditions can move a material from one family toward another.
The three panels in the picture name them: heat, sudden loading, and many cycles. Each one reshapes how the material fails.
First, heat. Many metals that are brittle when cold turn ductile when hot, which is exactly why a blacksmith heats iron in the forge before hammering it into shape.
Second, the rate of loading. Apply the load slowly and a metal may flow ductilely, but hit it with a sudden shock and even a normally ductile metal can behave brittlely and crack.

<whisper>Third, and the most dangerous, repeated cycling. Load and unload a part many times and it suffers elastic fatigue, gradually losing strength until it can fail well below its normal breaking stress.
This is not academic. It is precisely why aircraft parts and railway axles are retired on a fixed schedule of cycles, not just when they happen to look worn out.
So hold these labels loosely. Ductile, brittle, malleable are genuine material properties, but they are not frozen; temperature, loading rate, and fatigue all shift them.
numbers से पहले एक और concept: ये family labels पत्थर पर खुदे नहीं हैं। तीन conditions एक material को एक family से दूसरी की ओर सरका सकती हैं।
picture के तीन panels इन्हें नाम देते हैं: heat, sudden loading, और many cycles. हर एक बदल देता है कि material कैसे fail होता है।
पहला, heat. ठंडे में brittle कई metals गरम होने पर ductile हो जाते हैं, इसीलिए एक लोहार लोहे को हथौड़े से आकार देने से पहले भट्टी में गरम करता है।
दूसरा, loading की rate. load धीरे लगाइए और metal ductilely flow कर सकता है, पर उसे एक sudden shock से मारिए और एक सामान्यतः ductile metal भी brittlely behave करके crack कर सकता है।

<whisper>तीसरा, और सबसे ख़तरनाक, repeated cycling. एक part को कई बार load-unload कीजिए और वो elastic fatigue झेलता है, धीरे-धीरे strength खोते हुए जब तक वो अपने normal breaking stress से काफ़ी नीचे fail न कर जाए।
यह academic नहीं है। यही ठीक वजह है कि aircraft parts और railway axles cycles के एक fixed schedule पर retire किए जाते हैं, सिर्फ़ तब नहीं जब वो घिसे हुए दिखें।
तो इन labels को ढीला थामिए। ductile, brittle, malleable असली material properties हैं, पर वो frozen नहीं; temperature, loading rate, और fatigue सब इन्हें सरकाते हैं।

board_events.text: Linear region up to the proportional limit: Hooke's law holds, slope is Y, and unloading gives full recovery.
Elastic limit and yield point: the last point of full recovery, where large plastic flow begins.
Plastic region: strain grows fast for little extra stress, and unloading now leaves a permanent set.
Ultimate tensile strength: the peak stress; past it, a ductile sample necks, thinning locally.
Fracture point: the wire breaks, and the stress there is the breaking stress.

segments.text: Now the classification framework: how to walk the curve region by region and read a material off it. The picture labels every stop on the journey.
Trace it with me from the origin outward, because each region tells you something specific about the material.
First, the linear region, up to the proportional limit. Here stress is proportional to strain, Hooke's law holds, the slope is the Young's modulus, and if you unload the wire recovers fully.
Next, the elastic limit and yield point, which sit so close in many metals that we treat them as one. This is the last point of full recovery, and just beyond it large plastic flow begins.

Then the plastic region. Strain now grows rapidly for very little extra stress, and this is the defining behaviour: unload from here and the wire keeps a permanent set, the unloading line landing short of the origin.
Push on and you reach the ultimate tensile strength, the peak of the curve, the greatest stress the material can bear. Past the peak, a ductile sample necks, thinning locally at one spot.
<whisper>And finally the fracture point, where the wire actually breaks. The stress at that last point is the breaking stress, the end of the journey.
अब classification framework: curve को region दर region कैसे चलें और उससे material पढ़ें। picture यात्रा के हर पड़ाव को label करती है।
मेरे साथ origin से बाहर की ओर trace कीजिए, क्योंकि हर region आपको material के बारे में कुछ ख़ास बताता है।
पहला, linear region, proportional limit तक। यहाँ stress strain के proportional है, Hooke's law चलता है, slope Young's modulus है, और अगर आप unload करें तो wire पूरी तरह recover कर जाती है।
फिर, elastic limit और yield point, जो कई metals में इतने पास होते हैं कि हम उन्हें एक ही मानते हैं। यह full recovery का आख़िरी point है, और इसके ठीक आगे बड़ा plastic flow शुरू होता है।

फिर plastic region. strain अब बहुत थोड़े extra stress पर तेज़ी से बढ़ता है, और यही defining behaviour है: यहाँ से unload कीजिए और wire एक permanent set रखती है, unloading line origin से पहले उतरती हुई।
आगे बढ़िए और आप ultimate tensile strength तक पहुँचते हैं, curve का peak, वो सबसे बड़ा stress जो material झेल सकता है। peak के बाद, एक ductile sample neck करता है, एक जगह locally पतला होते हुए।
<whisper>और आख़िर में fracture point, जहाँ wire सचमुच टूटती है। उस आख़िरी point पर stress breaking stress है, यात्रा का अंत।

board_events.text: Both resilience and toughness are areas under the same curve, but bounded differently.
Resilience = area up to the yield point = energy stored elastically and fully recovered.
Toughness = area under the entire curve to fracture = total energy absorbed before breaking.
Springs and trampolines maximise resilience; crash barriers and helmets maximise toughness.
A material can be very resilient but not tough, or very tough but not especially resilient.

segments.text: The last concept is a beautiful contrast between two quantities that are both areas under the curve, yet mean opposite things.
The picture shows it directly: a small green wedge up to the yield point, and the whole shaded region out to fracture. Same curve, two different areas.
Both resilience and toughness are areas under the same stress-strain curve. The difference is entirely in where you stop measuring.
Resilience is the area under the curve up to the yield point. It is the energy stored elastically, the part that is fully recoverable. This is what springs and trampolines are designed to maximise.
Toughness is the area under the entire curve, all the way to fracture. It is the total energy absorbed before the material breaks. This is what crash barriers and helmets are designed to maximise.
<curious>So the design intent splits the two: choose a resilient material when you want the energy handed back, and a tough material when you want the energy absorbed and not returned.
And they are genuinely independent. A material can be very resilient but not tough, like a brittle spring steel, or very tough but not especially resilient, like a ductile structural metal.
आख़िरी concept दो quantities के बीच एक सुंदर contrast है जो दोनों curve के नीचे के areas हैं, फिर भी उल्टी चीज़ें बताते हैं।
picture इसे सीधे दिखाती है: yield point तक एक छोटा green wedge, और fracture तक पूरा shaded region. एक ही curve, दो अलग areas.
resilience और toughness दोनों एक ही stress-strain curve के नीचे areas हैं। फ़र्क़ पूरी तरह इसमें है कि आप नापना कहाँ रोकते हैं।
resilience है yield point तक curve के नीचे का area. यह elastically stored energy है, वो हिस्सा जो पूरी तरह recoverable है। springs और trampolines इसी को maximise करने के लिए बने हैं।
toughness है पूरी curve के नीचे का area, ठीक fracture तक। यह material के टूटने से पहले सोखी गई total energy है। crash barriers और helmets इसी को maximise करने के लिए बने हैं।
<curious>तो design का इरादा दोनों को बाँट देता है: resilient material चुनिए जब आप energy वापस चाहते हैं, और tough material जब आप energy सोखी और वापस न दी हुई चाहते हैं।
और ये सचमुच independent हैं। एक material बहुत resilient पर tough नहीं हो सकता, जैसे brittle spring steel, या बहुत tough पर ख़ास resilient नहीं, जैसे ductile structural metal.

sections.title: The anchoring quantities

board_events.text: The quantities that anchor this subtopic
Yield strength $\sigma_y$: the stress at the yield point, the boundary between elastic and plastic (unit Pa).
Modulus of resilience is the area under the elastic part: the safe elastic energy budget per unit volume.
Toughness is the total area under the curve to fracture: the total energy absorbed per unit volume.
Ductility (graphical) is the curve length from yield to ultimate; permanent set is the residual strain after unloading.
Resilience is the area up to yield; toughness is the whole area to fracture.

segments.text: This subtopic is mostly qualitative, but a handful of quantities anchor it, and here they are on one board.
First, yield strength, sigma y. It is simply the stress at the yield point, marking the boundary between elastic, recoverable deformation and plastic, permanent deformation, measured in pascals.
The one true formula here is the modulus of resilience: one half sigma y epsilon y, which also equals sigma y squared over two Y.
Read what that means: the modulus of resilience is the area under the elastic part of the curve, the safe elastic energy budget per unit volume, the most a material can store and still spring back.
Toughness is its bigger cousin: the total area under the entire curve to fracture, the total energy absorbed per unit volume before the material breaks.

Two more terms round it out. Ductility, read graphically, is the length of the curve from yield to the ultimate load; and permanent set is the residual strain left after loading past yield and unloading.
<excited>Keep the two areas straight and you have mastered half this subtopic: resilience is the area up to yield, toughness is the whole area to fracture.
यह subtopic ज़्यादातर qualitative है, पर कुछ quantities इसे anchor करती हैं, और यहाँ वो एक board पर हैं।
पहला, yield strength, sigma y. यह बस yield point पर stress है, जो elastic, recoverable deformation और plastic, permanent deformation के बीच सीमा है, pascals में नापी गई।
यहाँ एकमात्र सच्चा formula है modulus of resilience: one half sigma y epsilon y, जो sigma y squared बटा two Y के भी बराबर है।
इसका मतलब पढ़िए: modulus of resilience curve के elastic हिस्से के नीचे का area है, safe elastic energy budget per unit volume, वो सबसे ज़्यादा जो material store करके भी वापस उछल सके।
toughness इसका बड़ा cousin है: पूरी curve के नीचे fracture तक का total area, material के टूटने से पहले सोखी गई total energy per unit volume.
दो और terms इसे पूरा करते हैं। ductility, graphically पढ़ी गई, yield से ultimate load तक curve की length है; और permanent set yield के पार load करके unload करने के बाद बचा residual strain है।
<excited>दोनों areas को सीधा रखिए और आपने इस subtopic का आधा जीत लिया: resilience yield तक का area है, toughness fracture तक का पूरा area.

sections.title: CBSE: modulus of resilience

board_events.text: CBSE: modulus of resilience
Given yield strength 3.0e8 Pa and Young's modulus 2.0e11 Pa. Resilience is the energy density at the yield point.
Beyond this energy density the wire yields and will not fully recover: the safe elastic budget.
Notice it needs only the yield strength and Young's modulus, nothing about the wire's size.

segments.text: Let us make the one formula of this subtopic concrete with a board-level problem.

The data: a steel wire with a yield strength of three point zero times ten to the eight pascals and a Young's modulus of two point zero times ten to the eleven pascals. The modulus of resilience is just the energy density at the yield point.
So we use resilience equals sigma y squared over two Y, the elastic energy density evaluated right at yield.

Substitute. The numerator is three point zero times ten to the eight, squared, which is nine point zero times ten to the sixteen. The denominator is two times two point zero times ten to the eleven, which is four point zero times ten to the eleven.
Divide, and the modulus of resilience comes out to two point two five times ten to the five joules per cubic metre.
<curious>Read the meaning: beyond this energy density the wire would yield and not fully recover. So this number is the safe elastic energy budget for every cubic metre of the material.
And notice what the formula did not need: nothing about the wire's length, area, or shape. Resilience is a property of the material alone.
चलिए इस subtopic के एकमात्र formula को एक board-level problem से ठोस बनाते हैं।

data: yield strength three point zero times ten to the eight pascals और Young's modulus two point zero times ten to the eleven pascals वाली steel wire. modulus of resilience बस yield point पर energy density है।
तो हम इस्तेमाल करते हैं resilience बराबर sigma y squared बटा two Y, ठीक yield पर नापी elastic energy density.

substitute कीजिए। numerator है three point zero times ten to the eight, squared, जो है nine point zero times ten to the sixteen. denominator है two times two point zero times ten to the eleven, जो है four point zero times ten to the eleven.
divide कीजिए, और modulus of resilience निकलता है two point two five times ten to the five joules per cubic metre.
<curious>मतलब पढ़िए: इस energy density के पार wire yield कर जाती और पूरी तरह recover नहीं करती। तो यह number material के हर cubic metre का safe elastic energy budget है।
और देखिए formula को क्या नहीं चाहिए था: wire की length, area, या shape के बारे में कुछ नहीं। resilience सिर्फ़ material की property है।

sections.title: NEET: stiffness versus ductility

board_events.text: NEET: which is stiffer, which is more ductile?

board_events.caption: P rises steeply and ends early; Q is gentler and reaches far

<path d="M60,225 L130,60" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"/>
<circle cx="130" cy="60" r="3" fill="#b3402f"/><text x="130" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#b3402f">P: steep, snaps early</text>
<path d="M60,225 L170,150 C230,110 300,105 360,120" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"/>
<circle cx="360" cy="120" r="3" fill="#2b6ca3"/><text x="360" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#2b6ca3">Q: gentler, long reach</text>

board_events.text: Trap: assuming the steeper or higher curve is better in every way, or confusing stiffness with ductility.
Young's modulus is the slope of the linear part; P is steeper, so P has the greater Young's modulus.
Ductility is how far the curve extends before fracture; Q reaches much higher strain, so Q is more ductile.
Stiffness and ductility point to different materials; eliminate any option bundling them.
A stiff material can be brittle, and a flexible one ductile; the two are independent.

segments.text: Now a N E E T comparison that lives entirely in reading a graph correctly.
The picture shows two curves. P rises steeply and ends abruptly at a low strain; Q rises less steeply but continues to a much higher strain before fracturing.
The trap is baked in. Students assume the curve that goes higher or steeper is better in every respect, or they simply confuse stiffness with ductility.
Separate the two ideas cleanly. Young's modulus is the slope of the linear part. P is the steeper curve, so P has the greater Young's modulus, meaning P is the stiffer material.
Ductility is a different thing entirely: how far the curve extends before it fractures. Q reaches a much higher strain, so Q is the more ductile material, and P, snapping early, is the more brittle.

<excited>So stiffness and ductility point to opposite materials here. Eliminate on sight any option that bundles greater Young's modulus with more ductile for the same material; that is the planted error.
The takeaway generalises: a stiff material can be brittle, and a flexible one can be ductile. Stiffness and ductility are independent properties.
अब एक N E E T comparison जो पूरी तरह एक graph को सही पढ़ने में बसता है।
picture दो curves दिखाती है। P steeply चढ़ती है और कम strain पर अचानक ख़त्म होती है; Q कम steeply चढ़ती है पर fracture से पहले कहीं ज़्यादा strain तक जारी रहती है।
trap अंदर ही पका है। students मान लेते हैं कि जो curve ऊँची या steeper जाती है वो हर लिहाज़ से बेहतर है, या वो बस stiffness को ductility समझ लेते हैं।
दोनों ideas को साफ़ अलग कीजिए। Young's modulus linear हिस्से का slope है। P steeper curve है, तो P का Young's modulus ज़्यादा है, मतलब P stiffer material है।
ductility बिलकुल अलग चीज़ है: fracture से पहले curve कितनी दूर जाती है। Q कहीं ज़्यादा strain तक पहुँचती है, तो Q ज़्यादा ductile material है, और P, जल्दी snap होते हुए, ज़्यादा brittle.

<excited>तो stiffness और ductility यहाँ उल्टे materials की ओर इशारा करते हैं। जो option same material के लिए greater Young's modulus को more ductile के साथ बाँधे उसे देखते ही हटा दीजिए; वही planted गलती है।
सीख सामान्य है: एक stiff material brittle हो सकता है, और एक flexible वाला ductile. stiffness और ductility independent properties हैं।

board_events.text: Max load 2000 kg, yield strength 2.5e8 Pa, safety factor 5. Take g = 10 m/s-squared.
The safety factor keeps the cable working comfortably inside its elastic region.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main design problem that puts yield strength to practical use.
The picture sets it up: a lift cable must hold a load, but the working stress is deliberately kept to a fraction of the yield strength for safety.

The data: a maximum load of two thousand kilograms, a yield strength of two point five times ten to the eight pascals, and a safety factor of five, meaning the working stress must not exceed one fifth of the yield strength. Take g as ten metres per second squared.

First the force and the allowed stress. The force is m g, that is two thousand times ten, which is two point zero times ten to the four newtons. The working stress is the yield strength over five, which is five point zero times ten to the seven pascals.

Next the minimum area. It is the force over the working stress: two point zero times ten to the four over five point zero times ten to the seven, which is four point zero times ten to the minus four square metres.

Finally convert area to diameter. Using area equals pi d squared over four, the diameter is the square root of four A over pi, which comes out to about two point three times ten to the minus two metres, that is two point three centimetres.
<curious>Read the design intent: the safety factor of five keeps the cable working comfortably inside its elastic region, so under the rated load it never even approaches yielding.
अब एक J E E Main design problem जो yield strength को व्यावहारिक इस्तेमाल में लाता है।
picture इसे सजाती है: एक lift cable को load थामना है, पर working stress जानबूझकर safety के लिए yield strength के एक अंश तक रखा जाता है।

sections.title: JEE Advanced: strong, stiff and tough are independent

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: strong, stiff and tough are independent

board_events.text: Young's modulus is the slope of the initial line; A is steeper, so its modulus is greater. A is stiffer.
Breaking stress is the stress at fracture; A fractures high while B's plateau lies below, so A is stronger.
Ductility is the plastic extent; A snaps almost at once while B has a long plateau, so B is far more ductile.
Toughness is the total area; B's modest stress acts over a huge strain, so B is the tougher material.
Strong, stiff and tough are three independent properties: glass wins two, mild steel wins the others.

segments.text: The J E E Advanced closer is a reasoning problem, and its whole lesson is that three words we often blur together are actually independent.

The picture shows two materials. Curve A is a steep straight line to a high stress, then fracture almost at once. Curve B is a gentler line to a lower yield, then a long plastic plateau to large strain before fracture.

Take the four properties one at a time, each read off a specific feature. First, Young's modulus is the slope of the initial straight line. A is steeper, so the modulus of A is greater. A is the stiffer material.
Second, breaking stress is the stress at the fracture point. A fractures at a high stress, and B's entire plateau lies below that, so A has the greater breaking stress. A is the stronger material.
Third, ductility is the extent of plastic deformation, the curve length from yield to fracture. A snaps with almost no plastic region, while B has a long plateau, so B is far more ductile.

Fourth, toughness is the total area under the curve. Although A reaches a higher stress, its area is a thin sliver because it breaks at tiny strain; B's modest stress acts over a huge strain, enclosing a much larger area, so B is the tougher material.

<whisper>Here is the deep takeaway: strong, stiff, and tough are three independent properties. A glass rod is strong and stiff yet shatters without warning, while a mild-steel rod bends and absorbs enormous energy before failing, which is exactly why structural beams are made of the latter.
J E E Advanced closer एक reasoning problem है, और इसकी पूरी सीख यह है कि तीन शब्द जिन्हें हम अक्सर एक कर देते हैं, दरअसल independent हैं।

picture दो materials दिखाती है। curve A एक steep straight line है एक high stress तक, फिर लगभग तुरंत fracture. curve B एक gentler line है एक lower yield तक, फिर fracture से पहले large strain तक एक लंबा plastic plateau.
चारों properties को एक-एक करके लीजिए, हर एक किसी ख़ास feature से पढ़ी। पहला, Young's modulus initial straight line का slope है। A steeper है, तो A का modulus ज़्यादा है। A stiffer material है।
दूसरा, breaking stress fracture point पर stress है। A एक high stress पर fracture होता है, और B का पूरा plateau उससे नीचे है, तो A का breaking stress ज़्यादा है। A stronger material है।
तीसरा, ductility plastic deformation का विस्तार है, yield से fracture तक curve की length. A लगभग बिना plastic region के snap होता है, जबकि B का लंबा plateau है, तो B कहीं ज़्यादा ductile है।

चौथा, toughness curve के नीचे का total area है। भले ही A ऊँचे stress तक पहुँचे, इसका area एक पतली किरच है क्योंकि यह tiny strain पर टूटता है; B का modest stress huge strain पर act करता है, कहीं बड़ा area घेरते हुए, तो B tougher material है।

<whisper>यहाँ गहरी सीख है: strong, stiff, और tough तीन independent properties हैं। एक glass rod strong और stiff है फिर भी बिना चेतावनी चकनाचूर होता है, जबकि एक mild-steel rod मुड़कर fail होने से पहले भारी energy सोखता है, इसीलिए structural beams उसी से बनते हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and the read-in-order pro-tip

board_events.text: Pitfalls and one pro-tip
Ductility (wires, tension), malleability (sheets, compression) and elasticity (recovery) are three different properties.
'Rubber is more elastic than steel' is true only loosely; by Young's modulus, steel is more elastic.
The slope of the curve is Young's modulus (stiffness); areas are energies (resilience, toughness).
Yielding is the onset of permanent deformation, not breaking; a material can carry load through a long plastic range.
Pro-tip: decode each property from one feature, in order: slope, fracture height, horizontal extent, total area.
Running this fixed checklist stops you bundling stiff, strong and tough into one material.

segments.text: Let us close the subtopic with the traps it plants most reliably.

First, keep three properties distinct. Ductility is being drawn into wires, in tension; malleability is being hammered into sheets, in compression; and elasticity is the ability to recover. A material can rank differently on each.

Second, the famous line: rubber is more elastic than steel is true only in the loose everyday sense of large recoverable strain. By the physics definition, Young's modulus, steel is the more elastic. Know which definition the question wants.

Third, never mix up slope and area on the curve. The slope of the linear part is Young's modulus, the stiffness. Areas are energies: the area to yield is resilience, the total area to fracture is toughness.

Fourth, do not treat the yield point as fracture. Yielding is the onset of permanent deformation, not breaking. A material can yield and keep carrying load through a long plastic range before it finally fractures.

<excited>And the pro-tip that organises every two-curve question: decode each property from one specific feature, and always in the same order. Slope gives stiffness, the fracture height gives strength, the horizontal extent past yield gives ductility, and the total enclosed area gives toughness.
Running that fixed checklist, every time, stops you from bundling stiff, strong, and tough into one material when the graph is deliberately separating them.
चलिए subtopic को उन traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो यह सबसे भरोसेमंद तरीके से बोता है।

पहला, तीन properties को अलग रखिए। ductility है wires में खींचा जाना, tension में; malleability है sheets में पीटा जाना, compression में; और elasticity है recover करने की क्षमता। एक material हर एक पर अलग rank कर सकता है।

दूसरा, वो मशहूर line: rubber steel से ज़्यादा elastic है, सिर्फ़ large recoverable strain के ढीले रोज़मर्रा अर्थ में सच है। physics की definition, Young's modulus से, steel ज़्यादा elastic है। जानिए सवाल कौन सी definition चाहता है।
तीसरा, curve पर slope और area को कभी मत मिलाइए। linear हिस्से का slope Young's modulus है, stiffness. areas energies हैं: yield तक का area resilience, fracture तक का total area toughness.
चौथा, yield point को fracture मत मानिए। yielding permanent deformation की शुरुआत है, टूटना नहीं। एक material yield करके भी fracture से पहले एक लंबे plastic range में load ढो सकता है।

<excited>और वो pro-tip जो हर two-curve सवाल को व्यवस्थित करता है: हर property को किसी एक ख़ास feature से decode कीजिए, और हमेशा एक ही क्रम में। slope stiffness देता है, fracture height strength देता है, yield के आगे horizontal extent ductility देता है, और total enclosed area toughness देता है।
उस fixed checklist को हर बार चलाना आपको stiff, strong, और tough को एक material में बाँधने से रोकता है जब graph जानबूझकर इन्हें अलग कर रहा हो।

board_events.text: Atoms rest at the bottom of a potential well, at the separation $r_0$ where their forces balance.
Displace an atom slightly and the well acts like a tiny spring: restoring force grows with displacement.
Summed over trillions of bonds, this linear response is the macroscopic Hooke's law, sigma = Y epsilon.
Young's modulus is large when bonds are stiff (metals, diamond), small when floppy (rubber's coiling chains).
It also explains why Hooke's law holds only for small strains: stretch far and the parabola breaks.

segments.text: This final subtopic puts the whole chapter to work, but it opens by answering the question we have carried since the very beginning: why is a solid elastic at all?
The picture holds the answer. Plot the potential energy of two neighbouring atoms against their separation, and you get a well, a curve with a clear minimum.
Every atom sits at the bottom of that well, at the equilibrium separation r naught, the distance where the attractive and repulsive forces exactly balance.
Now displace an atom slightly. Near the bottom, the well is shaped like a parabola, and a parabola behaves exactly like a spring: the restoring force grows in proportion to the displacement.

Make that precise. Expand the energy near r naught as a parabola, and the force, minus the slope of the energy, comes out linear in the displacement, minus kappa times r minus r naught. That is a spring of stiffness kappa.
<curious>Now multiply this over the trillions of atomic bonds across a wire, and the collective linear response is nothing other than the macroscopic Hooke's law, sigma equals Y epsilon.

It even explains the size of Young's modulus. Y is large when the bonds are stiff, as in metals and diamond, and small when they are floppy, as in rubber, where long molecular chains uncoil rather than stretching their bonds.
And it explains the fine print we kept quoting: Hooke's law holds only for small strains. Stretch far enough and the parabola approximation, and eventually the bond itself, simply breaks.
यह आख़िरी subtopic पूरे chapter को काम पर लगाता है, पर यह उसी सवाल से खुलता है जो हम शुरू से ढो रहे हैं: solid elastic है ही क्यों?
picture जवाब थामे है। दो पड़ोसी atoms की potential energy को उनके separation के सामने plot कीजिए, और मिलता है एक well, एक साफ़ minimum वाला curve.
हर atom उस well की तली में बैठा है, equilibrium separation r naught पर, वो दूरी जहाँ attractive और repulsive forces बिलकुल balance होते हैं।
अब एक atom को थोड़ा displace कीजिए। तली के पास, well एक parabola जैसा है, और parabola बिलकुल spring की तरह behave करता है: restoring force displacement के proportion में बढ़ता है।

इसे सटीक बनाइए। energy को r naught के पास parabola के रूप में expand कीजिए, और force, energy का minus slope, displacement में linear निकलता है, minus kappa times r minus r naught. यह kappa stiffness की एक spring है।
<curious>अब इसे एक wire के trillions atomic bonds पर गुणा कीजिए, और यह मिलाजुला linear response macroscopic Hooke's law, sigma बराबर Y epsilon, के अलावा कुछ नहीं है।

यह Young's modulus का size भी समझाता है। Y बड़ा होता है जब bonds stiff हों, जैसे metals और diamond में, और छोटा जब वो floppy हों, जैसे rubber में, जहाँ लंबी molecular chains bonds खींचने के बजाय खुलती हैं।
और यह वो fine print समझाता है जो हम बार-बार बताते रहे: Hooke's law सिर्फ़ small strains पर चलता है। काफ़ी दूर खींचिए और parabola approximation, और आख़िरकार bond ख़ुद, टूट जाता है।

How much it sags depends on the load, the material, and, dramatically, the shape of the cross-section.

board_events.text: Material near the neutral axis barely works, so scoop it out: the I-section.
For a rectangle $I_g = bd^{3}/12$, so depth matters far more than breadth, since $\delta \propto 1/d^{3}$.

segments.text: Every structure you trust is a negotiation with elasticity, and the first negotiation is the humble beam.

The picture shows what bending really is. Load a beam in the middle and it bows: its lower fibres stretch under tension, its upper fibres squeeze under compression, and a neutral layer in between neither stretches nor shrinks.
So a beam is tension on one side and compression on the other, with a stress-free layer down the middle.
How far it sags, the depression, depends on the load and the material, but above all on the shape of the cross-section, and that is where the engineering lives.

The formulas capture it: for a cantilever loaded at its free end, the depression is W L cubed over three Y I g; for a beam on two supports with a central load, it is W L cubed over forty-eight Y I g. Here I g is the geometrical moment of the cross-section.

<excited>Now look at this second picture, because it is one of the great engineering insights. Since the material near the neutral axis barely carries any stress, you can scoop it out and pile that material far from the centre instead.
That is exactly the I-section. Same stiffness, far less weight, which is why steel girders, railway tracks, and aircraft spars are all I-shaped or hollow.

And the reason depth beats breadth: for a rectangle the geometrical moment is b d cubed over twelve, so the depression falls as one over depth cubed but only as one over breadth. Always stand a beam on its long edge.
हर structure जिस पर आप भरोसा करते हैं वो elasticity से एक सौदा है, और पहला सौदा है विनम्र beam.

picture दिखाती है bending असल में है क्या। एक beam को बीच में load कीजिए और वो झुकती है: इसके निचले fibres tension में खिंचते हैं, ऊपरी fibres compression में दबते हैं, और बीच में एक neutral layer न खिंचती है न सिकुड़ती।
तो एक beam एक तरफ़ tension और दूसरी तरफ़ compression है, बीच में एक stress-free layer के साथ।
यह कितनी झुकती है, depression, load और material पर निर्भर है, पर सबसे बढ़कर cross-section की shape पर, और यहीं engineering बसती है।

formulas इसे पकड़ते हैं: अपने free end पर load हुई cantilever के लिए, depression है W L cubed बटा three Y I g; दो supports पर central load वाली beam के लिए, यह है W L cubed बटा forty-eight Y I g. यहाँ I g cross-section का geometrical moment है।

<excited>अब इस दूसरी picture को देखिए, क्योंकि यह महान engineering insights में से एक है। चूँकि neutral axis के पास का material मुश्किल से कोई stress झेलता है, आप उसे scoop out करके वो material केंद्र से दूर ढेर कर सकते हैं।
यही I-section है। same stiffness, कहीं कम weight, इसीलिए steel girders, railway tracks, और aircraft spars सब I-shaped या hollow होते हैं।

और depth breadth को क्यों हराता है: एक rectangle के लिए geometrical moment है b d cubed बटा twelve, तो depression घटता है one over depth cubed पर सिर्फ़ one over breadth. beam को हमेशा उसके लंबे किनारे पर खड़ा कीजिए।

board_events.text: Rock at the base of a mountain bears the weight of everything above it.
The base cannot bear more than the rock's breaking stress; beyond it the rock flows or crumbles.
For rock this is about 10 km, which is why Everest is the size it is and not ten times bigger.

segments.text: The second application is a beautiful order-of-magnitude argument: elasticity sets a ceiling on how tall a mountain can be.
The picture is the model. Treat the mountain as a column of rock, and the rock right at the base has to bear the entire weight of everything stacked above it.
So the compressive stress at the base is the weight of the overlying rock divided by the area.
Work it out and the area cancels: the base stress is simply rho g h, the rock's density times g times the height. Taller mountain, more stress at the base.
But the base cannot bear an unlimited stress. Once it exceeds the rock's breaking, or compressive, stress, the rock at the bottom yields and flows, and the mountain cannot grow further.
Set the base stress equal to that maximum, and the greatest possible height is sigma max over rho g. A clean formula for a mountain's ceiling.
<curious>Put in numbers for rock and you get about ten kilometres, which comfortably brackets the tallest mountains on Earth. That is why Everest is the size it is, and not ten times bigger.
दूसरा application एक सुंदर order-of-magnitude तर्क है: elasticity तय करती है कि एक mountain कितना ऊँचा हो सकता है।
picture ही model है। mountain को rock का एक column मानिए, और ठीक base पर की rock को ऊपर टिके सब कुछ का पूरा weight झेलना है।
तो base पर compressive stress है ऊपरी rock का weight बटा area.
इसे हल कीजिए और area cancel हो जाता है: base stress बस rho g h है, rock की density times g times height. ऊँचा mountain, base पर ज़्यादा stress.
पर base असीमित stress नहीं झेल सकता। एक बार यह rock के breaking, या compressive, stress को पार करे, तली की rock yield करके flow करती है, और mountain आगे नहीं बढ़ सकता।
base stress को उस maximum के बराबर रखिए, और सबसे ज़्यादा संभव height है sigma max बटा rho g. एक mountain की छत का साफ़ formula.
<curious>rock के लिए numbers रखिए और मिलता है लगभग दस किलोमीटर, जो Earth के सबसे ऊँचे mountains को आराम से घेरता है। इसीलिए Everest उतना ही है जितना है, दस गुना बड़ा नहीं।

board_events.text: Heat a free rod and it lengthens by $\Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T$, a thermal strain $\alpha\Delta T$.
Clamp both ends so it cannot expand; the walls supply an equal and opposite mechanical strain $\alpha\Delta T$.

board_events.latex: \sigma = Y\varepsilon = Y\alpha\Delta T, \qquad F = \sigma A = YA\alpha\Delta T

board_events.text: Neither expression contains L: a short clamped rod and a long one develop the same thermal stress.
This is why rails have gaps, bridges sit on roller supports, and pipelines have expansion loops.

segments.text: The third application shows heat acting as a hidden mechanical force, one strong enough to buckle steel.
The picture sets the scene: a rod clamped rigidly between two fixed walls, then heated. It wants to expand, but the walls will not let it.
Start with a free rod. Heat it and it lengthens by L times alpha times delta T, which is a thermal strain of alpha times delta T, where alpha is the coefficient of linear expansion.

Now clamp both ends so it cannot actually expand. To hold it at its original length, the walls must supply exactly the compression that cancels that expansion, an equal and opposite mechanical strain of alpha delta T.
By Hooke's law the stress required is Y times that strain, so the thermal stress is Y alpha delta T, and the force on each support is that stress times the area, Y A alpha delta T.
<whisper>And here is the striking feature: neither expression contains the length L. A short clamped rod and a long one develop exactly the same thermal stress for the same temperature change.

This is not abstract. It is precisely why railway tracks are laid with gaps, why bridges rest on roller supports, and why long pipelines are built with expansion loops, all so that heat can move the metal without shattering the structure.
तीसरा application heat को एक छिपे mechanical force की तरह दिखाता है, इतना मज़बूत कि steel को मोड़ दे।
picture दृश्य सजाती है: एक rod जो दो fixed walls के बीच rigidly clamped है, फिर गरम की गई। यह expand करना चाहती है, पर walls इसे नहीं देतीं।
एक free rod से शुरू कीजिए। इसे गरम कीजिए और यह L times alpha times delta T जितनी लंबी होती है, जो alpha times delta T का thermal strain है, जहाँ alpha coefficient of linear expansion है।

अब दोनों सिरे clamp कीजिए ताकि यह सचमुच expand न कर सके। इसे इसकी original length पर रोकने के लिए, walls को ठीक वो compression देना है जो उस expansion को cancel करे, alpha delta T का equal और opposite mechanical strain.
Hooke's law से ज़रूरी stress है Y times वो strain, तो thermal stress है Y alpha delta T, और हर support पर force है वो stress times area, Y A alpha delta T.
<whisper>और यहाँ चौंकाने वाली बात है: किसी भी expression में length L नहीं है। एक short clamped rod और एक long, same temperature change के लिए बिलकुल same thermal stress पैदा करते हैं।

यह abstract नहीं है। यही ठीक वजह है कि railway tracks gaps के साथ बिछाए जाते हैं, bridges roller supports पर टिकते हैं, और लंबी pipelines expansion loops के साथ बनती हैं, ताकि heat metal को हिला सके बिना structure तोड़े।

board_events.text: Fix one end and twist the other through angle $\theta$; a shell at radius $x$ is sheared by $\phi = x\theta/L$.
Its shear stress is $\tau = \eta\phi$; the moment of the ring's tangential force about the axis is $dC = \tau\,(2\pi x\,dx)\,x$.
The R-to-the-fourth dependence is why a modest increase in shaft radius dramatically stiffens it.
Torsional rigidity, the torque per unit twist, is $\pi\eta r^{4}/2L$.

segments.text: The fourth application is torsion, how a rod resists being twisted, and it is where the shear modulus finally earns its keep.
The picture shows the trick: imagine the cylinder as a set of thin coaxial shells, and analyse one shell at a time.
Fix one end and twist the other through an angle theta. A shell at radius x is sheared, and geometry gives its shear angle as phi equals x theta over L, larger for shells farther out.

That shell carries a shear stress tau equal to eta times phi. Its tangential force acts on a ring of area two pi x d x, and the moment of that force about the axis is tau times two pi x d x, times x again.
Integrate that moment from the centre out to the radius R. The integral of x cubed gives R to the fourth over four, and the total torque comes out to pi eta R to the fourth theta, over two L.
<curious>Now savour the R to the fourth. Because the torque scales as the fourth power of the radius, even a modest increase in shaft thickness stiffens it enormously against twisting.
We name the torque per unit twist the torsional rigidity, pi eta r to the fourth over two L, and it is why drive shafts and axles are made as fat as the weight budget allows.
चौथा application है torsion, एक rod मुड़ने को कैसे resist करती है, और यहीं shear modulus आख़िरकार अपनी कमाई करता है।
picture trick दिखाती है: cylinder को पतले coaxial shells के एक समूह की कल्पना कीजिए, और एक बार में एक shell का विश्लेषण कीजिए।
एक सिरा fix कीजिए और दूसरे को angle theta से घुमाइए। radius x पर एक shell sheared होता है, और geometry इसका shear angle देती है phi बराबर x theta बटा L, बाहर वाले shells के लिए बड़ा।

वो shell एक shear stress tau झेलता है जो eta times phi के बराबर है। इसका tangential force two pi x d x area की एक ring पर लगता है, और axis के गिर्द उस force का moment है tau times two pi x d x, times x फिर से।
उस moment को केंद्र से radius R तक integrate कीजिए। x cubed का integral देता है R to the fourth बटा four, और total torque निकलता है pi eta R to the fourth theta, बटा two L.
<curious>अब R to the fourth का मज़ा लीजिए। चूँकि torque radius की चौथी power के हिसाब से बढ़ता है, shaft की मोटाई में मामूली बढ़ोतरी भी उसे मुड़ने के ख़िलाफ़ ज़बरदस्त stiff कर देती है।
torque per unit twist को हम torsional rigidity कहते हैं, pi eta r to the fourth बटा two L, और इसीलिए drive shafts और axles उतने मोटे बनाए जाते हैं जितना weight budget इजाज़त दे।

board_events.text: Measuring Y: Searle's experiment

board_events.caption: A reference wire beside the experimental wire cancels stray errors
