board_events.text: Hang two identical wires from the same support: a reference wire with a fixed load, and the experimental wire.
A frame with a spirit level and a micrometer measures the difference in their elongations.
Add known loads, level the bubble, record the extension, and plot load against extension: a straight line.
The reference wire cancels temperature and support errors: both wires shift together.
Measure the radius carefully: since $Y \propto 1/r^{2}$, a small radius error is doubled in the result.

segments.text: The last application is the one you meet in the laboratory: Searle's experiment, the standard way to actually measure Young's modulus.
The picture shows the apparatus, and its clever feature is that there are two wires, not one, hanging side by side from the same rigid support.
One is a reference wire, carrying a fixed dead load just to keep it taut. The other is the experimental wire, the one we will load and study.
The two are joined by a frame carrying a spirit level and a micrometer screw, so that any tilt of the frame measures the difference in how much the two wires have stretched.

The procedure is to add known loads to the experimental wire in steps, level the spirit bubble with the micrometer each time, and record the extension. Plot load against extension and, within the elastic limit, you get a straight line.
From the slope of that line, Young's modulus is M g L over pi r squared delta L, the same working formula we derived right back in subtopic one.

<curious>Now, why two wires? Because the reference wire automatically cancels errors from temperature change and any yielding of the support. Both wires drift together, so only the load-induced stretch is measured.

One warning the picture flags in red: measure the radius separately and carefully. Because Young's modulus goes as one over radius squared, a small error in the radius is doubled in your final answer.
आख़िरी application वो है जो आप laboratory में मिलते हैं: Searle's experiment, Young's modulus को सचमुच नापने का standard तरीका।
picture apparatus दिखाती है, और इसकी चतुर बात यह है कि दो wires हैं, एक नहीं, एक ही rigid support से अगल-बगल लटकी हुई।
एक है reference wire, बस taut रखने के लिए एक fixed dead load ढोती हुई। दूसरी है experimental wire, जिसे हम load करके पढ़ेंगे।
दोनों एक frame से जुड़ी हैं जो spirit level और micrometer screw ढोता है, ताकि frame का कोई भी tilt इस फ़र्क़ को नापे कि दोनों wires कितनी खिंचीं।

procedure है experimental wire पर known loads steps में जोड़ना, हर बार micrometer से spirit bubble level करना, और extension record करना। load को extension के सामने plot कीजिए और, elastic limit के अंदर, मिलती है एक straight line.
उस line के slope से, Young's modulus है M g L बटा pi r squared delta L, वही working formula जो हमने subtopic one में ही derive किया था।

<curious>अब, दो wires क्यों? क्योंकि reference wire temperature change और support के किसी yielding से errors अपने आप cancel कर देती है। दोनों wires साथ drift करती हैं, तो सिर्फ़ load से हुआ stretch नापा जाता है।

एक चेतावनी जो picture red में उठाती है: radius को अलग से और सावधानी से नापिए। चूँकि Young's modulus one over radius squared के हिसाब से चलता है, radius में छोटी गलती आपके final answer में दुगनी हो जाती है।

sections.title: The applications toolkit and reference data

board_events.text: Applications toolkit and reference data

board_events.latex: \sigma_{\text{thermal}} = Y\alpha\Delta T, \qquad F = YA\alpha\Delta T \quad(\text{no } L)

board_events.text: Reference: steel Y about 200, copper 120, aluminium 70, rubber 0.01 to 0.1 gigapascals.

segments.text: Here is the full applications toolkit on one board, the reference for the four worked examples ahead.
First, beam depression. For a cantilever loaded at its free end it is W L cubed over three Y I g; for a beam on two supports with a central load it is W L cubed over forty-eight Y I g.
The geometrical moment I g is b d cubed over twelve for a rectangle, and pi r to the fourth over four for a circle, and the depression goes as one over depth cubed.
Second, the mountain ceiling: the maximum height is sigma max over rho g.
Third, thermal stress: Y alpha delta T, with the force Y A alpha delta T, and remember neither contains the length.
Fourth, torsion and measurement: the torque is pi eta r to the fourth theta over two L, and Searle's experiment gives Young's modulus as M g L over pi r squared delta L.

<curious>And keep these orders of magnitude in mind: Young's modulus is about two hundred gigapascals for steel, one hundred twenty for copper, seventy for aluminium, and just zero point zero one to zero point one for rubber.
यहाँ पूरा applications toolkit एक board पर है, आगे के चार worked examples का reference.
पहला, beam depression. अपने free end पर load हुई cantilever के लिए यह है W L cubed बटा three Y I g; दो supports पर central load वाली beam के लिए W L cubed बटा forty-eight Y I g.
geometrical moment I g एक rectangle के लिए b d cubed बटा twelve है, और एक circle के लिए pi r to the fourth बटा four, और depression one over depth cubed के हिसाब से चलता है।
दूसरा, mountain की छत: maximum height है sigma max बटा rho g.
तीसरा, thermal stress: Y alpha delta T, force Y A alpha delta T के साथ, और याद रखिए किसी में length नहीं है।
चौथा, torsion और measurement: torque है pi eta r to the fourth theta बटा two L, और Searle's experiment Young's modulus देता है M g L बटा pi r squared delta L.

<curious>और इन orders of magnitude को याद रखिए: Young's modulus steel के लिए लगभग two hundred gigapascals है, copper के लिए one hundred twenty, aluminium के लिए seventy, और rubber के लिए बस zero point zero one से zero point one.

sections.title: CBSE: maximum height of a mountain

board_events.text: CBSE: maximum height of a mountain
Breaking stress 3.0e8 Pa, density 2.5e3 kg per cubic metre, g = 10. The base stress must not exceed the breaking stress.
Reassuringly close to the scale of the tallest mountains on Earth.
Higher gravity gives shorter mountains, which is why low-gravity Mars hosts Olympus Mons.

segments.text: Let us cash in the mountain formula on a board-level estimate.

The data: a rock with a breaking compressive stress of three point zero times ten to the eight pascals and a density of two point five times ten to the three kilograms per cubic metre, with g of ten. The base stress rho g h must not exceed that breaking stress.
So the maximum height is simply the breaking stress over rho g.

Substitute: three point zero times ten to the eight, over the product of two point five times ten to the three and ten, which is three point zero times ten to the eight over two point five times ten to the four.
That comes out to one point two times ten to the four metres, which is twelve kilometres.
<curious>Reassuringly, that is right around the scale of the tallest mountains on Earth, a lovely check on a one-line estimate.
And the formula carries a bonus insight: higher gravity gives shorter mountains, which is exactly why low-gravity Mars can host Olympus Mons, a volcano far taller than anything on Earth.
चलिए mountain formula को एक board-level estimate पर भुनाते हैं।

data: three point zero times ten to the eight pascals के breaking compressive stress और two point five times ten to the three kilograms per cubic metre की density वाली rock, g ten के साथ। base stress rho g h उस breaking stress से ज़्यादा न हो।
तो maximum height बस breaking stress बटा rho g है।

substitute कीजिए: three point zero times ten to the eight, बटा two point five times ten to the three और ten का product, जो है three point zero times ten to the eight बटा two point five times ten to the four.
यह निकलता है one point two times ten to the four metres, जो है बारह किलोमीटर।
<curious>राहत की बात, यह Earth के सबसे ऊँचे mountains के पैमाने के ठीक आसपास है, एक one-line estimate पर बढ़िया check.
और formula एक bonus insight ढोता है: ज़्यादा gravity छोटे mountains देती है, इसीलिए कम-gravity वाला Mars, Olympus Mons को थाम सकता है, Earth के किसी भी चीज़ से कहीं ऊँचा एक volcano.

sections.title: NEET: length-free thermal stress

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: thermal stress
A steel rod clamped between fixed walls is heated by 40 degrees Celsius. Y = 2.0e11 Pa, alpha = 1.2e-5 per degree.
Trap: students hunt for the rod's length and area, assuming a longer or thinner rod gives a different stress.
It is independent of length; only the force, stress times area, would need the area.
If a NEET option changes the answer when the length is doubled, eliminate it on sight.
Clamping cancels the expansion, so the stress needs only Y, alpha and delta T.

segments.text: Now a N E E T speed trap on thermal stress, built to punish anyone who reaches for the wrong variables.

The data: a steel rod clamped rigidly between two fixed walls, then heated so its temperature rises by forty degrees Celsius, with Young's modulus two times ten to the eleven pascals and a coefficient of expansion of one point two times ten to the minus five per degree.
The trap is right there. Students go hunting for the rod's length and cross-section, assuming a longer or a thinner rod must give a different stress. It does not.
The thermal stress is Y alpha delta T: two times ten to the eleven, times one point two times ten to the minus five, times forty, which is nine point six times ten to the seven pascals.
<excited>And notice what the answer did not use: neither the length nor the area. The stress is independent of length; only the force, stress times area, would ever need the area.
So the exam radar is simple. If a N E E T option changes the answer when the length is doubled, eliminate it on sight, because length cannot enter.
The whole idea is that clamping cancels the expansion, so the stress that develops needs only three things: Young's modulus, the expansion coefficient, and the temperature change.
अब thermal stress पर एक N E E T speed trap, जो गलत variables उठाने वाले को सज़ा देने के लिए बना है।

data: दो fixed walls के बीच rigidly clamped एक steel rod, फिर इतनी गरम की गई कि इसका temperature forty degrees Celsius बढ़े, Young's modulus two times ten to the eleven pascals और expansion coefficient one point two times ten to the minus five per degree के साथ।
trap वहीं है। students rod की length और cross-section ढूँढते हैं, मानते हुए कि एक longer या thinner rod अलग stress देगी। नहीं देती।
thermal stress है Y alpha delta T: two times ten to the eleven, times one point two times ten to the minus five, times forty, जो है nine point six times ten to the seven pascals.
<excited>और देखिए answer ने क्या इस्तेमाल नहीं किया: न length न area. stress length से independent है; सिर्फ़ force, stress times area, को कभी area चाहिए होता।
तो exam radar सरल है। अगर कोई N E E T option length दुगनी होने पर answer बदले, उसे देखते ही हटा दीजिए, क्योंकि length आ ही नहीं सकती।
पूरा idea यह है कि clamping expansion को cancel कर देती है, तो जो stress पैदा होता है उसे सिर्फ़ तीन चीज़ें चाहिए: Young's modulus, expansion coefficient, और temperature change.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main beam problem that makes the depth-cubed rule concrete.
The picture also carries the lesson: turn this beam on its side and it sags far more. But first the numbers.

The data: a cantilever one metre long, with a rectangular cross-section of breadth four centimetres and depth six centimetres, a load of two hundred newtons at the free end, and Young's modulus two times ten to the eleven pascals. Two steps: first the geometrical moment, then the depression.

That works out to about four point six times ten to the minus four metres, or zero point four six millimetres.

<curious>And here is the payoff of the depth-cubed rule: if you turned the beam on its side, so the depth were only four centimetres, the depression would rise by six over four, squared, that is two point two five times. sections.title: Pitfalls and the power-law pro-tip

board_events.text: Pitfalls and one pro-tip
Thermal stress $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$ has no length; length sets the prevented expansion, not the stress.
The beam $I_g$ is the area moment $\int y^{2}\,dA$ in metres to the fourth, not the rotational $\sum m r^{2}$.
For a rectangle depression goes as $1/d^{3}$ but only $1/b$: doubling depth is eight times as effective as breadth.
Both beam stiffness and torsional rigidity scale as $r^{4}$, so small radius changes have outsized effects.
Pro-tip: for any 'change a dimension' question, write the power law and take the ratio.
Most exam questions on this subtopic secretly just test whether you know the exponent.

segments.text: Let us close the subtopic with its favourite traps and a single unifying pro-tip.

First, the length trap. Thermal stress is Y alpha delta T, with no length in it at all. The length only sets how much the rod would have expanded if free; it never sets the stress once expansion is prevented.

Second, do not confuse the two moments of inertia. The I g in beam formulas is the area moment, the integral of y squared d A, measured in metres to the fourth. It is not the rotational moment, sum of m r squared, from mechanics. Same name, different quantity.

Third, remember depth and breadth are not equal partners. For a rectangular beam, the depression goes as one over depth cubed but only as one over breadth, so doubling the depth is eight times as effective as doubling the breadth.

Fourth, watch the fourth-power laws. Both beam stiffness, through the circular area moment, and torsional rigidity scale as the radius to the fourth, so even small changes in radius have outsized effects, and a small radius error wrecks a Young's modulus measurement.

<excited>And now the pro-tip that ties the whole subtopic together: for any question that changes a dimension, do not recompute from scratch. Write the proportionality, take the ratio, and read off the answer in one line.
Because, honestly, most exam questions on this subtopic are secretly just testing whether you know the exponent: one over depth cubed, radius to the fourth, or no length at all.
चलिए subtopic को इसके पसंदीदा traps और एक ही unifying pro-tip के साथ बंद करते हैं।
पहला, length trap. thermal stress है Y alpha delta T, इसमें length है ही नहीं। length सिर्फ़ यह तय करती है कि free होने पर rod कितनी expand करती; expansion रुकने के बाद यह stress कभी तय नहीं करती।

दूसरा, दो moments of inertia को मत मिलाइए। beam formulas में I g area moment है, y squared d A का integral, metres to the fourth में नापा। यह mechanics वाला rotational moment, sum of m r squared, नहीं है। same नाम, अलग quantity.

तीसरा, याद रखिए depth और breadth बराबर साझेदार नहीं हैं। एक rectangular beam के लिए, depression one over depth cubed के हिसाब से चलता है पर सिर्फ़ one over breadth, तो depth दुगना करना breadth दुगना करने से आठ गुना असरदार है।

चौथा, fourth-power laws का ध्यान रखिए। beam stiffness, circular area moment के ज़रिए, और torsional rigidity दोनों radius to the fourth के हिसाब से चलते हैं, तो radius में छोटे बदलाव भी बड़ा असर डालते हैं, और radius में छोटी गलती एक Young's modulus measurement बिगाड़ देती है।
<excited>और अब वो pro-tip जो पूरे subtopic को बाँधता है: किसी भी सवाल के लिए जो dimension बदलता है, शुरू से मत compute कीजिए। proportionality लिखिए, ratio लीजिए, और answer एक line में पढ़िए।
क्योंकि, सच कहें तो, इस subtopic के ज़्यादातर exam questions चुपके से बस यह test करते हैं कि आप exponent जानते हैं या नहीं: one over depth cubed, radius to the fourth, या length बिलकुल नहीं।

sections.title: Chapter 8 formula recap

board_events.text: Chapter 8: formula recap

segments.text: Before the final cheat sheet, let us sweep the whole chapter's formulas onto one board, subtopic by subtopic.
The foundations first: stress is force over area, strain is a dimensionless fractional change, and Hooke's law ties them as sigma equals E epsilon.

The four constants: Young's modulus F L over A delta L, bulk modulus minus P over fractional volume change with compressibility one over B, rigidity shear stress over shear strain, and Poisson's ratio minus lateral over longitudinal strain.
The moduli at work: a wire is a spring of stiffness Y A over L; combine reciprocals in series and stiffnesses in parallel; and two equal rods in series give two Y one Y two over the sum.

The gas and the constant relations: isothermal bulk modulus P, adiabatic gamma P, and the binding relations, Y equals two eta one plus nu equals three B one minus two nu, with nine over Y equals one over B plus three over eta.

Poisson and energy: fractional volume change one minus two nu times strain; stored energy one half F delta L; energy density one half sigma epsilon, or sigma squared over two Y; and sudden loading doubles the static stretch.
The material budget and self-weight: modulus of resilience sigma y squared over two Y, self-weight elongation M g L over two A Y, and the maximum hanging length sigma break over rho g.

board_events.text: Chapter 8: rapid-recall cheat sheet
More Y, more elastic: steel beats rubber. Strain is dimensionless, never in pascals.
Wire equals spring, $k = YA/L$: short and fat is stiff. Series adds stretches; parallel adds stiffness.
Slow gas is soft ($B=P$), fast gas is stiff ($B=\gamma P$). Only two of the four constants are free.
Stretch it, it slims (that is $\nu$). Half the force: $U=\tfrac{1}{2}F\Delta L$. Drop it and it doubles: $x_{max}=2x_{static}$.
Slope is stiffness, area is energy, length is ductility, loop is lost heat.
Depth cubed, breadth single. Heat builds stress, not by the metre. Twist loves $r^{4}$. Mountains end where rock gives way.
Milestones in order: Proportional, Elastic, Yield, Ultimate, Fracture. 'Please Eat Your Usual Food.'

segments.text: And now the whole chapter distilled into a rapid-recall cheat sheet, the lines to carry into the exam hall.
Start with the golden rule from subtopic one: more Young's modulus means more elastic, so steel beats rubber, and strain is dimensionless, never carrying pascals.
From the moduli subtopic: a wire is a spring of stiffness Y A over L, so short and fat is stiff. Series adds the stretches; parallel adds the stiffnesses.
For gases and constants: a slow gas is soft, with bulk modulus P, a fast gas is stiff, with gamma P, and only two of the four elastic constants are ever independent.
From Poisson and energy: stretch it and it slims, that is Poisson's ratio; elastic energy uses half the force, so U is one half F delta L; and a suddenly dropped load doubles the static stretch.
From the yielding subtopic, the four-word reading of any curve: slope is stiffness, area is energy, length is ductility, and an enclosed loop is lost heat.

<excited>And the applications, in four punchy lines: depth cubed and breadth single for beams; heat builds stress but not by the metre; twist loves the fourth power of radius; and mountains end where the rock gives way.
Finally, the milestones of the stress-strain curve, in order: Proportional, Elastic, Yield, Ultimate, Fracture. Remember them as, Please Eat Your Usual Food. That is Chapter Eight, start to finish.
और अब पूरा chapter एक rapid-recall cheat sheet में निचोड़ा हुआ, वो lines जो exam hall में ले जानी हैं।
subtopic one के golden rule से शुरू: ज़्यादा Young's modulus मतलब ज़्यादा elastic, तो steel rubber को हराता है, और strain dimensionless है, कभी pascals नहीं ढोता।
moduli subtopic से: एक wire, Y A बटा L stiffness की एक spring है, तो short and fat is stiff. series stretches जोड़ता है; parallel stiffnesses जोड़ता है।
gases और constants के लिए: एक slow gas soft है, bulk modulus P के साथ, एक fast gas stiff है, gamma P के साथ, और चार elastic constants में से सिर्फ़ दो ही कभी independent होते हैं।
Poisson और energy से: खींचिए और यह पतला होता है, वो Poisson's ratio है; elastic energy आधा force लेती है, तो U है one half F delta L; और अचानक गिराया load static stretch को दुगना करता है।
yielding subtopic से, किसी भी curve का चार-शब्द पाठ: slope stiffness है, area energy है, length ductility है, और एक enclosed loop lost heat है।

<excited>और applications, चार दमदार lines में: beams के लिए depth cubed और breadth single; heat stress बनाता है पर metre के हिसाब से नहीं; twist को radius की चौथी power पसंद है; और mountains वहाँ ख़त्म होते हैं जहाँ rock give way करती है।
आख़िर में, stress-strain curve के milestones, क्रम में: Proportional, Elastic, Yield, Ultimate, Fracture. इन्हें ऐसे याद रखिए, Please Eat Your Usual Food. यह रहा Chapter Eight, शुरू से आख़िर तक।
